# Raw Initializer External Slice Proposal

First, consider raw initializers and External Slice within the same compatibility window. Both can easily get waved through with "the model can still be read": the former may already have changed its text representation, while the latter may have found the file without reading the original range.

The previous investigation initially stopped at `onnx/defs/parser.h`. Start there to look for declarations related to text objects and adjacent calls, but don't yet assume external file handling belongs to this path. We haven't yet verified whether file location, offset, and length are interpreted elsewhere.

Two tasks are planned.

- Create a raw initializer round-trip sample, retaining the input object, printed text, and TensorProto after reading it back. The focus isn't on how nice the text looks, but on whether type-specific element representations were changed along the way.
- Create a sample where the external file is larger than the target segment, so the effects of offset and length are visible. If the file length exactly matches the read length, even a whole-file read would be hard to spot.

Both can also be put into a combined model, but we shouldn't report only a single "pass" result. A combined model is useful for reproducing the environment, not for replacing separate assessments: the text being accepted doesn't mean the object read back is the same; the file existing doesn't mean the read range is correct.

The tentative plan is to retain two separate artifacts first, then decide whether a combined sample is needed. If the raw initializer portion can only be read back by changing the existing representation, it will not be included in this round; if the External Slice portion only works when the model directory or range fields are ignored, it should not be submitted as a compatibility result either.

Open: whether legacy callers depend on the slice's offset and length or only on the final content; this still needs to be checked by following the references.

# Raw Initializer External Slice Proposal

The first draft treated "the printer can emit it," "the parser can accept it," "the external file is readable," and "the slice is still correct" as one claim. Separate these checks first during review. They can all apply to one model, but their failure points differ and should not be covered by a single success indicator.

## Trade-offs retained from the first draft

The first version proposed one large sample: a text graph containing initializers, with the model also referencing a segment of data in an external file. This has a practical advantage. Readers only need to open one input to see all the objects relevant to the compatibility window together.

The problem is that a large sample makes the checks less discriminating. If the parser accepts the output text, that does not establish that the initializers are still represented as before; if the external file can be opened, that does not establish that the offset and length actually affect the read. A slice that happens to span the entire file could even make an implementation that ignores the range fields look correct.

The original recommendation for a combined sample has therefore been kept, but as supporting material. Its only role is to preserve the combined scenario. Raw initializers and External Slice should each have their own observation points; the review must not use one as a substitute for the other.

## Initializer track

Here, "raw initializers" is not a blanket term for all TensorProto. It refers to objects in the compatibility window that cannot first be converted to a display-friendly numeric form with the expectation that the reader will infer the original meaning. int8 and float16 are two cases that need particular care: for the former, the sign changes an element's meaning; for the latter, the displayed numeric value does not inherently represent the original storage unit.

There are two possible approaches.

The first is to have the output side emit readable numeric values wherever possible, and have the reader restore them according to type. The advantage is readable text and potentially a smaller scope of changes. The problem is that once the output has erased a type-dependent distinction, the reader has no reliable information with which to restore it; the final "read succeeded" result will hide the change in representation.

The second is to have the output side and the reader use a common representation that allows comparison for samples confirmed to require a raw round trip. This does not require converting every initializer to a low-level format, nor does it turn the two existing examples into a rule for all types. It only requires that the content retained in the sample not be silently altered during printing.

We are leaning toward the second approach. The corresponding sample record needs to retain three things together: the TensorProto in the input, the actual text emitted by the printer, and the TensorProto after parsing again. Looking only at the numeric values on screen is not enough, and neither is keeping only a piece of text. Element order must also be checked, because a change in order may not immediately make the type or length look wrong.

## External Slice track

External Slice must not be described simply as "external data support." This round only covers Regular External File within the model directory, and whether the location and length in the metadata still refer to the same segment of content. File access and range interpretation should be recorded separately.

The file-access question is whether the target can be located relative to the model directory. The range question is whether the read starts at the specified position and stops after the specified length. The former can be correct while the latter is still wrong; conversely, having the expected segment correct in memory does not establish that file access itself stayed within the directory.

The earlier investigation used `onnx/defs/parser.h` as a starting point for verification. This location is still useful for navigating to neighboring text objects, but the path name does not establish that external files are opened there or that slice reads happen there. Follow-up work needs to trace the actual references to identify the file-handling entry point; until then, the document retains only the navigation hint to "start looking from the parser side."

One suggested shortcut was to read all the external data into memory first, then compare it with the expected TensorProto. This can help inspect the final content, but it does not show whether offset and length were actually respected. If the whole file happens to match the expected content, or an incorrect range still lands on the same elements, the check may pass. This approach can be kept for temporary troubleshooting, but it is not an acceptance criterion for this round.

Another approach is to check only that the target file exists. This is useful for detecting missing files or an incorrect model directory, but it cannot replace the slice check either. New samples should have a target file larger than the required segment and make the full file and the specified segment produce different initializer results; otherwise, the range fields are not actually being observed.

## Scope for this round

This round does not include symlinks, Parent Directory Link, or other path cases in the slice sample. Those cases affect the boundaries of file access, but the existing material does not indicate whether conclusions about range issues for regular files should also apply to them. Adding them just to make the sample look complete would only conflate path errors and range errors again.

Nor is this page meant to be a general explanation of the external data mechanism. The goal here is narrower: preserve the text round-trip observations for raw initializers, and enable an independent review of whether legacy calls retain External Slice results. If further investigation finds no direct relationship between the file-access entry point and the parser path, narrow the navigation guidance here rather than forcing in a claim about which component owns the implementation.

## Proceed or withdraw

The recommendation is to prepare two independent samples first, then consider a combined sample. If the initializer sample fails, the record should state whether the change occurred in the printed text or in the object read back; if the slice sample fails, it should state whether the problem is file resolution, range interpretation, or a mismatch in the final content read. That way, even if changes are made in different places, reviewers do not have to guess at the cause from a single large sample.

Withdrawal conditions should also be separate. If raw initializers can only be read again by rewriting their existing representation, withdraw the text round-trip part and return to discussing the format choice. If External Slice can only pass by ignoring the model directory, ignoring the position, or treating the entire file as the target segment, withdraw the slice part; do not call that relaxation compatibility with legacy calls.

Three questions remain open: whether the existing samples cover only the two initializer types mentioned here; whether the combined model is still worth keeping once the independent samples are stable; and whether there is still a type boundary between the bytes read by External Slice and the interpretation of TensorProto that needs to be called out separately.

# Raw Initializer External Slice Plan

This record has remained in IR-18 Compatibility Window for a long time. It was not originally a complete design, but a review note that tied together two easily overlooked observations: after a text round trip, the raw initializer still appeared readable; an external data reference still appeared able to open the file. The later problem was not whether these two statements were completely wrong, but that they made it too easy to stop at "readable" and "openable," overlooking whether the object was preserved and whether the range was preserved.

The two objects in the title meet in the same model, but there is no reason to require them to share a single implementation entry point, nor to let one regression result vouch for both semantics. The trail of the raw initializer runs through the text printer, parser, and TensorProto; the trail of External Slice runs through the model directory, Regular External File, position, and length. An earlier investigation used `onnx/defs/parser.h` as its starting point; this starting point can still be used to find text-related adjacent objects, but it is no longer used as the basis for deciding file-processing ownership.

The earlier paragraphs below have not been cleaned up into the current documentation. The working assumptions from several follow-up notes, the shortcuts that were withdrawn, and the old samples have all been retained, because people may still encounter these approaches through old branches or old links. The current proposal appears later; read it in the context of these records first.

## 2023-06-26: Initial Combined-Sample Concept

The initial draft only wanted to retain the raw initializer example from the user report, while also ensuring that the fact that an old call retained the External Slice result was not lost. At the time, the most direct approach was to prepare a combined model: the text graph would contain an initializer, and the model data would in turn point to an external file. If the input could be parsed, the output could be parsed again, and the file could be read for its contents, that seemed sufficient to show that the compatibility window had no obvious break.

At the time, the assessment was that a combined sample would be easier to review than two scattered samples. There was only one model and only one reproduction environment; if someone traced back from the output, they could see the text object and the external reference in the same place. This assessment still holds for "retaining one combined scenario," but it later became clear that it could not carry the full burden of validation.

Another assumption in the initial draft was: since the printer's output could be accepted by the parser, the raw initializer would probably have no problems either. The "probably" here was not unpacked at the time. Acceptance of the text showed, at most, that the reader had not immediately rejected it; it did not answer whether, during output, some type-related representation had been changed into another form, nor whether the element semantics of the read-back object matched those of the original object.

External Slice was also described too simplistically. The initial draft treated "the external file is still readable" as a sign that slicing was still working. This assessment was later narrowed: finding the file is just one observation at the entry point, and does not show that reading starts at the specified offset or ends after the specified length. If a sample happens to have a file whose length equals the expected length, reading the whole file and slicing correctly may even yield the same result.

The initial draft did not commit to using the same textual form for all TensorProto types, nor did it commit to covering all external data paths. It left only one practical direction to pursue: first bring samples that can expose the differences into review, then decide where to make changes. This boundary remains in place to this day, preventing a compatibility-window review ticket from being expanded into an unreliable global description.

## 2023-10-31: Redrawing the boundaries during review

The first formal reassessment did not immediately settle on changing the printer, parser, or external-file entry point. What changed first was the unit of review: rather than taking "one model round-tripped successfully" as the sole conclusion, the review was divided into a raw-initializer track and a External Slice track based on the questions readers needed answered.

The raw-initializer track needed to answer this: whether, given an existing TensorProto, the object obtained after passing it through the text printer and then reading it with the parser still represents the same set of elements. There are at least two kinds of observations here that cannot substitute for one another. The first is the output text, because the format itself may be what the reader actually sees; the second is the object read back, because an acceptable piece of text may still be interpreted as a different value. Element order should also be examined alongside these, and the comparison must not be limited to type names or element counts.

The External Slice track needed to answer this: whether, when a Regular External File in the model directory is referenced, the offset and length still point to the segment expected by the legacy call. There are likewise two kinds of observations here. Whether the file can be located is an entry-point issue; whether the range fields are interpreted is a reading issue. Writing both up as "external data is working" leaves no way to tell, after a failure, whether to start investigating the directory, the file, or the metadata.

The review did not divide the two tracks by directory or personnel. Their division was based on failure modes, not on who was more likely to modify the code. The cost of this approach is that subsequent commits may touch different locations, and reviewers also have to read them separately; the benefit is that text changes will not be misclassified as file changes, or file-entry failures misattributed to the parser, just to keep a single change tidy.

This review retained the combined sample, but downgraded it to a reproduction scenario. Only if standalone samples have already provided results for text round-tripping and range reads, respectively, does the combined model have a chance to show whether the two kinds of objects affect each other when present together. If it merely stitches together two examples that have already passed, the information it provides is not enough to offset the maintenance cost.

## 2023-11-01: Gaps left by review comments

The reviewed version did not interpret "raw" as arbitrary raw bytes, nor did it expand "External Slice" to encompass all path-safety policies. The former is concerned with ensuring that existing initializers in the compatibility window are not silently replaced by a convenience display at the textual level; the latter is concerned with ensuring that the file range old callers need to retain is not obscured by reading the entire file.

One unresolved question in the comments was whether the sample should record only the final TensorProto, or must also record the printer's intermediate text. In the end, "keep only the result" was not chosen. The reason is simple: if the text itself has already lost content capable of distinguishing representations, then even if the final object comparison happens to be identical, it cannot show that the formatting interface has not changed. Conversely, text alone cannot guarantee that the parser's interpretation has not deviated.

Another gap is the exact location of the external-file entry point. `onnx/defs/parser.h` is the earliest path encountered in the old investigation, making it suitable as a starting point for searching outward from the declaration and adjacent calls; opening the file path, directory boundaries, and range reads, however, cannot be concluded from this filename alone. Places in the old version where "look from the parser direction" was interpreted as "determined by the parser" should thereafter all be understood as navigation notes.

This annotation was not completed into a call-chain diagram. Without sufficient material, drawing a complete chain would only create conclusions harder to clean up than a gap. The retained approach is: for text differences, start by examining parser-adjacent objects; for External Slice differences, first confirm the target file, position, and length separately. The actual processing entry point is determined by what is found by following references.

## Legacy approach retained in the 2024 year: read the entire file and compare afterward

Someone once suggested reading the external file completely into memory first, then comparing it with the expected TensorProto content. This approach is tempting for temporary investigation: it reduces file-related environment variables, and the final values are easy to place side by side. Early records at one point described it as a shortcut implementation for the External Slice sample.

This approach is now marked **deprecated**, but not deleted. The problem is not that loading into memory is necessarily wrong, but that it removes the ability to observe whether the data is read by slices. If the implementation actually reads the entire file and then happens to obtain the same batch of elements through another method, the content comparison may still pass. At that point, the sample can only prove that certain data can be obtained; it cannot prove that offset and length still have semantics.

The legacy approach still has value for investigating the file contents themselves. When file corruption, missing content, or an incorrect model directory is suspected, observing the entire file can help narrow the scope. However, it should not serve as the basis for adopting this proposal, nor should it be written into the regression materials as the sole pass condition. The current slice sample must make the entire file and the target fragment produce distinguishable results.

Another related old recommendation was to check only that the external file exists. It has not been completely abandoned either: whether the target is in the model directory and whether the file can be located are still among the first conditions to check. But "existence" only answers the entry-point question, not the question of range. If the documentation only says "the file can be opened", readers should understand this as a limited observation, not a conclusion that slicing is correct.

## Another old practice retained in 2024: only checking whether the text can be read again

The check for raw initializers used to be even shorter: feed the printer output back to the parser, and count it as a pass as long as it is accepted. This check is useful for detecting obvious lexical, delimiter, or formatting breaks, so early sample A is still retained on the old branch.

It cannot confirm that the raw representation has been preserved. Acceptance of the text indicates, at most, that lexical and syntactic checks did not reject it at the entry point; it cannot establish whether signed integers are still interpreted with the same meaning, nor whether half-precision content still corresponds to the original storage units. If the output side first rewrites the information as a different, seemingly reasonable numerical value, the parser's success makes the problem harder to detect.

Therefore, old sample A can now serve only as a quick screening check. It can no longer support the conclusion that "initializer round-trips are stable" on its own. Whenever a judgment about the compatibility window is needed, the input object, the actual output text, and the read-back TensorProto must be kept side by side; if any of the three is missing, only a more limited observational conclusion should be drawn.

This is not a proposal to display every initializer in a hard-to-read format. The available material is insufficient to establish a formatting strategy for all types. The review is limited to samples that already require preservation of the raw representation; if other data types have similar risks, those risks should be demonstrated using their own inputs, text, and read-back objects, rather than extrapolated from two examples.

## 2025-09-08: Blind spots found while organizing the old examples

During this cleanup, the design of the early samples was re-examined, rather than merely checking whether they were still in the repository. The gap in old example A is that it only checks whether the printer output goes back into the parser, without requiring the read-back TensorProto to be compared with the input object in the same place. It can still help detect obvious formatting breaks, but cannot expose cases where "the text is readable but the object has changed".

The gap in old example B is that the external file length is exactly equal to the expected read length. It is useful for confirming that the minimal file can be found, but cannot distinguish "reading by range" from "always reading the entire file". Even if the implementation ignores the position and length, the result may happen to be the same. This example should not be deleted, because older troubleshooting may still need it to identify a missing file; however, it can no longer be called a slicing sample.

Taken together, the two old examples show exactly why this page does not use a single pass indicator. A short sample does not mean it has little semantic content. If the variables being changed do not actually affect the result, the test is merely confirming conditions that have not changed. Raw initializer samples must make differences in representation visible; External Slice samples must make the read range visible.

While organizing this material, we also confirmed a boundary that remains unresolved: slicing regular files is not the same issue as symbolic links and Parent Directory Link. The former first requires examining the range fields, while the latter primarily concerns path boundaries. They may intersect in later work on file entry points, but there is currently no material to support documenting them as a single rule or the same class of failure. To avoid reader confusion, this page uses only regular files as the starting point for slice samples.

## Side Notes from a Review

A seemingly simple question came up during the review: if the final numeric values are equal, why care about the original form? At the time, we did not turn this into a slogan, but instead broke it down into two concrete checks: whether the output text can express the same set of elements; and whether parsing it again yields the same kind of TensorProto interpretation. The former prevents the output stage from losing distinguishing information, while the latter prevents the reading stage from changing the interpretation.

Another question was whether path safety and slicing correctness could be checked in a single check. The conclusion was not to merge the two, but to acknowledge that they fail at different points. When the target goes outside the model directory, the primary issue is the entry-point boundary; when the file is correct but the read range is wrong, the primary issue is metadata interpretation. A composite model can trigger these conditions at the same time, but the error records and review conclusions should still be written separately.

At the time, there was also a suggestion to "convert External Slice to inline data, then have the text pipeline handle everything uniformly". It was not pursued further. Doing so would change the conditions under which legacy calls preserve External Slice results, and would also remove file ranges from the scenario being examined. If a future discussion concerns migration to inline data, this can be raised again; within the current compatibility window, it is not a way to preserve legacy behavior.

The review notes did not expand these side notes into a full explanation of the mechanism. Readers only need to be able to start investigating from three entry points: the raw initializer, External Slice, and `onnx/defs/parser.h`. Implementation ownership, call relationships, and error branches beyond these three objects should be verified at the specific references, and should not be filled in ahead of time on this page.

## Current Options

There are still two options to compare for raw initializers. Option one keeps the existing output conventions and puts as much compatibility handling as possible on the read side. Its advantage is that the changes are concentrated in one area, and the legacy output path appears unaffected; the risk is that if the output has already rewritten the original information, the read side can only interpret what remains and cannot reliably recover distinctions that were never written out.

Option two applies only to the initializer entries within this review's scope that have already been confirmed to require round-tripping, and explicitly states that output and input should preserve the same set of comparable representations. It makes the format an interface surface that needs review, and also requires the samples to check both text and objects. The cost is that compilation or basic parsing alone is not enough; the benefit is that it is easier to tell whether a failure occurred during output or reading.

There are also two options for External Slice. The first compares only the content ultimately read, which has a low preparation cost, but cannot tell whether the position and length are still being honored. The second makes the external file larger than the target slice and ensures that the complete file and the target range produce different results. The second requires a little more sample preparation, but can directly distinguish between reading the entire file and reading the specified range.

The current leaning is toward option two's initializer-handling approach and the second External Slice sample. Here, "leaning" does not constitute a decision on all implementation details. The actual file-opening entry point, how failure information should be presented, and whether directory boundaries should be included in the same round of changes all still depend on later references and samples. The proposal fixes here only the observation points that must not be sacrificed for convenience.

## Materials to retain before adoption

The original initializer sample should leave the input object, printer output, and read-back TensorProto next to one another. The record need not become a long log, but it must not retain only "pass". If the output text can no longer distinguish representations that originally had to be preserved, then even if a runtime's displayed value appears close, it cannot be considered stable at the text level.

The External Slice sample should clearly identify the target file in the model directory and state that the referenced range is not the entire file. This does not require a single example to cover all path boundaries; it only requires the sample to make "reading the complete file" and "reading the specified segment" produce different results. If the record only proves that the file was found, the conclusion may only state that the file entry point is usable; if the record only proves that the final contents are identical, the conclusion likewise cannot be expanded to say that the range field is already covered.

The two samples should be able to fail independently. When the initializer fails, it should be possible to tell whether the discrepancy is in the text, element order, or read-back object. When slicing fails, it should be possible to tell whether the problem is file location, position, length, or the final content obtained. This will not reduce the number of subsequent changes, but it can prevent one large sample from collapsing different faults into a single failure that is difficult to review.

## Current proposal

The current proposal sets preservation requirements for only two interface surfaces. The first is the original initializer's text round trip: the output side must retain enough information for the reading side to restore the same object, and the check must cover both the actual text and the read-back TensorProto. The second is External Slice: when Regular External File is referenced within the model directory, the sample must make the interpretation of position and length independently observable; file readability cannot substitute for range correctness.

The public text format of the original initializer must preserve the signed int8 sequence {1,-2,127,-128} and the float16 bit patterns {15360,49152,14336}, and the TensorProto numeric values obtained by parsing again must not change.

This requirement applies only to the raw initializer samples already established in this review. It does not propose using the same textual form for all data types, nor does it bring all external-data cases onto this page. int8 must preserve the signed decimal meaning of its elements; float16 must preserve its 16-bit storage bit pattern; neither may change after reparsing because the output side chose a different presentation.

External Slice is still handled within a narrower scope. Regular-file samples come before symbolic links and Parent Directory Link; file entry points come before broader path rules; position and length come before inferences about all TensorProto external encodings. This order is not intended to put off the issues, but to ensure that each sample actually answers the question it was set up to answer.

## Fallback points if this is not adopted

If an initializer can only be reread by changing its existing representation, the text round-trip portion should not be included in the compatibility window, and discussion should return to the choice of format. "Reading an approximately equal numeric value" cannot be treated as preserving the original representation.

If External Slice can pass only by ignoring the model directory, treating position or length as optional information, or treating the entire file as the target content, the slicing portion should be withdrawn. Such relaxations would change the assumptions underlying the scope preserved for legacy calls and cannot be presented as compatibility.

If following the references reveals that `onnx/defs/parser.h` only provides unrelated declaration navigation, then its description here should be narrowed further to a legacy troubleshooting entry point, and should no longer imply that it contains text-reading or file-handling implementations. This condition does not change the requirements for the raw initializers or External Slice themselves; it only prevents the document from misrepresenting a starting point as a conclusion about ownership.

## Remaining related questions

Whether a combined sample is needed is still undecided. Separate samples can already expose text round-tripping and range interpretation individually; a combined sample is worth maintaining only if it can show that the two actually affect each other. If it merely puts two examples that have already passed into the same model, it adds little information.

Whether symbolic links and Parent Directory Link need to be listed separately after regular-file slicing has not been decided on this page either. Those cases involve path boundaries, and conclusions about them cannot be inferred from regular-file samples simply because the words "external file" appear in both.

Finally, one question remains unanswered: once the bytes read from a slice reach initializer interpretation, are there any boundaries that need to be listed separately by type. The current proposal only requires that comparable TensorProto can ultimately be observed, and does not assume that all types or all forms of external encoding have already been covered. Keeping this question open is intended to prevent "the range is correct" from later being misread as "all external representations of initializers have been handled".

# Lexical and locale node-attribute troubleshooting tree

When graph text fails to read and node attributes appear to be missing, record them as two separate symptoms first; don't classify them together at the first step. The old troubleshooting lead is at `onnx/defs/parser.h`; this records the branches that the IR-18 sample could take at the time, not a complete reading guide.

The initial working assumption was that failures around special floating-point values were probably related to locale. After switching the environment to a setting that uses a period as the decimal separator, the text at hand did proceed further once. This only shows that the environment change affected that text; it does not show that quotes, comments, and whitespace are irrelevant. If graph, input, or output names are quoted, preserve them as-is first. Also don't remove comments or extra whitespace just to make reproduction easier.

```text
Read failure
├─ Cannot yet confirm that a node was formed
│  ├─ Text contains quoted identifiers
│  │  └─ Keep the complete fragment before and after the name
│  ├─ Text contains comments or extra whitespace
│  │  └─ Don't format it first; record the location of the anomaly
│  └─ Anomaly is near a special floating-point token
│     └─ Record the locale and the original lexeme
│
└─ A node exists, but its attributes do not appear as expected
   ├─ Save the node text and attribute section
   └─ First confirm that the node was not produced from normalized input
```

At the time, people would replace special values with ordinary numbers and then check whether the node appeared. This can expose a later path, but it cannot determine whether the original text stopped at lexical recognition, numeric conversion, or attribute reading. In particular, don't record success with the replacement as proof that the original input passed.

`inf` must be preserved as the original lexeme; don't change it to another numeric form in the record. If only formatted text remains, it is impossible to determine which lexical boundary it originally occupied.

Stop conditions: if there is no original graph text, no actual locale, or no way to confirm that the failure occurred before node formation, stop at the lexical branch. If the node fragment and attribute section are missing, don't guess the attribute names or default values.

# Troubleshooting tree for lexing, locale, and node attributes

This record still starts with `onnx/defs/parser.h`, but after review, we no longer treat it as a catch-all for every anomaly. Two kinds of reports often come in together here: in one, reading stops partway through the graph text; in the other, the text already produces nodes, and only then do incorrect attribute results show up. Both kinds mention quotes, comments, whitespace, and special floating-point forms, so early triage merged them into a single path.

## Sequence from the old page

The old rule from 2023 was to switch the locale first, then clean up the input. It came from a text sample that no longer failed at the same point after an environment change. Deleting comments, collapsing whitespace, and removing quotes from names were later folded into the same operation.

```text
Old procedure
├─ Switch locale
├─ Delete comments
├─ Clean up extra whitespace
├─ Remove quotes around identifiers
└─ Check node attributes if processing can continue
```

This sequence can no longer be used to determine the cause, but is being kept for now. When all four actions happen at once, all we know is that the rewritten text reached a different point; we cannot tell which action shifted the failure location. Removing quotes changes the lexical boundaries of names; deleting comments and collapsing whitespace also change how adjacent text is separated. Calling all these changes a "locale fix" was the clearest case of overattribution on the old page.

Another old conclusion also needs to be retained and flagged: once the text has passed through the read entry point, the remaining symptoms are an attribute-reading problem. The review found that this skips two checks: whether nodes have actually formed, and whether those nodes came from the same, unmodified input. Reaching the entry point does not mean nodes are available for attribute reading; seeing nodes does not mean the earlier lexical conditions played no part in the result.

## On-call follow-up notes

During the on-call review, we switched to capturing the material first, then choosing a branch. If no nodes have been produced yet, save only the original graph text, the snippet around the failure, the actual locale, and the error text. If nodes already exist but the attributes are not as expected, also save the node snippet and the attribute section. Do not collapse these two sets of material into "attributes not read," since that could mean no nodes formed, attributes are missing, attribute values are wrong, or reading stopped near the attributes.

Do not start by renaming quoted graph, input, and output identifiers. They may not be the cause of the anomaly, but once the quotes are removed manually, the original text boundaries are gone. The same applies to comments: the input after deletion can be kept for comparison, but cannot replace the text as it was when the anomaly occurred. If a formatter normalizes away extra whitespace, later node snippets may no longer correspond to the input as originally written.

At the time, we tried replacing special floating-point forms with ordinary decimal values, then checking whether the attributes appeared. That experiment did not produce a finding we could use directly. Replacing the values changed both lexeme classification and numeric interpretation; even if nodes were then present, we could not infer that the original lexemes had been read correctly. The result after replacement is therefore recorded only as "rewritten sample continued," not as "the original issue has been pinpointed."

## A reproduction run that did not separate the symptoms

One reproduction run changed only the locale, leaving the rest of the text intact. The results did not consistently split the symptoms into two groups: some text samples still stopped near comments or whitespace, while others reached the node stage before showing attribute differences. The material from that run was not enough to assign the cause to either the lexical branch or the attribute branch.

This does not mean locale has been ruled out. It only shows that changing the environment alone did not produce a consistent dividing line among the symptoms at hand. The old record interpreted this failed attempt as "the environment is not a factor"; we no longer use that claim. The claim that the environment still has an effect cannot be written up as proven either.

Another issue exposed during reproduction was that the source of the node snippets was not always clearly recorded. Some checks were done after deleting comments, others after removing quotes from names. Nodes obtained this way can help locate sensitive points, but cannot be compared directly with the original failure. If the nodes did not come from the same original text, differences in attribute reading should not be used to explain that original text's behavior.

## Troubleshooting tree now in use

```text
Graph text or node attribute anomaly found
│
├─ No confirmation yet that nodes have been produced
│  ├─ Anomaly near a quoted name
│  │  └─ Save the name, surrounding whitespace, and adjacent text; do not rename it first
│  ├─ Anomaly near comments or extra whitespace
│  │  └─ Keep the original section; deletion or cleanup must be a separate comparison
│  ├─ Anomaly near a special floating-point token
│  │  └─ Record the actual locale and the lexeme exactly as written; do not overwrite it with an ordinary value
│  └─ Failure location unclear
│     └─ First confirm whether nodes have formed; stay on this branch if that cannot be confirmed
│
└─ Nodes have been produced, but attribute results are wrong
   ├─ Nodes came from unmodified input
   │  ├─ Save the node snippet and attribute section
   │  └─ Record missing attributes, abnormal values, and interrupted reading separately
   ├─ Nodes came from cleaned-up text
   │  └─ Save as a new sample; do not use it directly to attribute a cause to the original anomaly
   └─ Verbal report only, no node snippet
      └─ Stop; do not guess attribute names
```

"Nodes have been produced" in the tree is a stopping point, not an assertion about implementation layers. Until that point has been passed, chasing attribute names usually just mixes earlier and later symptoms in the record. Conversely, once nodes have appeared, do not just go back and adjust the locale; first confirm whether the node text and attribute section still come from the same unmodified input.

## Gaps retained during review

The review did not require deleting the old steps. Some people still reach this page through the old "switch locale" lead, so the old procedure is retained, but it may only be used to identify historical samples, not to support a new causal attribution on its own. Environment adjustments, comment deletion, whitespace cleanup, quote changes, and numeric replacements are all different input conditions; they cannot be collapsed into a single success or failure.

Node Attribute Reading still has an unresolved area: after the text has passed the preceding stage, this record does not have the material to determine which attribute differences come from the original text and which come from its interpretation during reading. When adding samples later, save the failing text or output bytes, and state clearly whether nodes formed. If the material supports only "lexing and attribute reading have not yet been separated," stop at that statement; do not write up either side as a proven cause.

# Troubleshooting tree for lexing, locale, and node attributes

This page was initially treated as a broad entry point: cases where graph text could not be read, or where nodes already appeared to exist but attributes did not appear as expected, were all directed here. The two symptoms look similar on the surface and are often accompanied by quoted names, comments, extra whitespace, and special floating-point notation; older records therefore called them the same kind of "parsing anomaly". This page still retains that old entry point and terminology because troubleshooters will use them to find past samples, not because the old terminology is already precise enough.

The path for starting a direct check is still `onnx/defs/parser.h`. In the early material, it was merely a navigation point where lexical issues and node attribute issues met. Do not infer from this path alone that all attribute anomalies are handled in the same place, and do not skip the input text just because the issue name contains "attributes". During troubleshooting, first answer a narrower question: whether any nodes had already been formed from the unmodified input when the anomaly occurred.

Preserved below is a troubleshooting record with marginal notes added year by year. The old content has not been turned into a set of current rules, and some passages no longer apply; they still explain why it was later required to retain samples first, then run single-variable controlled comparisons.

## 2023-06: The initial working rules

Reading the earliest text received stopped near a special floating-point value. The observation available at the time was that, after switching to a locale that uses a period as the decimal separator, reading no longer stopped at the same point. So the old page named locale as the primary cause and gave a quick but insufficiently cautious sequence:

```text
Text reading anomaly
├─ Switch locale
├─ Delete comments
├─ Collapse extra whitespace
├─ Remove quotes around names
└─ Check node attributes once reading can continue
```

The practical purpose of this sequence was to let people see the node fragments further along as quickly as possible; that was also its problem. The environment and the input were changed at the same time, so any instance of "continuing" could only show that the rewritten text had reached the next stage. It could neither show that the original anomaly had disappeared nor that locale was what took effect first.

Removing quotes is not harmless cleanup. The symbols around graph names, input names, and output names determine where identifiers begin and end. Deleting comments is not harmless cleanup either: the position of comments relative to adjacent identifiers or numeric values is precisely the text boundary that needs to be observed. Collapsing extra whitespace into a uniform format also changes the input. The old rules performed these actions together, so it was impossible to distinguish which action had changed the symptom.

The early records also contained a statement that was later frequently quoted: "Once past the read entry point, what remains is an attribute issue." At the time, this was intended to remind troubleshooters not to keep focusing on the environment, but it collapsed several observation points into one too early. Text entering an entry point, nodes being constructed, and attributes being read each require different evidence to confirm. Without intermediate fragments, you cannot infer from "the error is not at the beginning" that nodes have already been formed, nor from "the attributes are not visible" that attribute reading must have executed.

This version of the old rules has not been deleted, because some historical reproductions left behind only its keywords. When you now see the clue "switch locale first", treat it as a past experiment rather than a current criterion for making a determination.

## Additional handwritten notes beside the old samples

Later, a simple constraint was added in the margin of an old page: do not save the cleaned-up text first. If a quoted name is manually renamed, the original lexical boundaries are lost; if comments are deleted before saving, their relationship to the preceding and following lexemes cannot be recovered; if whitespace is absorbed by a formatting tool, there is no way to know what the input actually looked like when the anomaly occurred.

This addendum did not lay out a complete procedure; it only required preserving the original text. Its starting point was not the assumption that every quote, comment, or whitespace character was a cause, but the need to avoid deleting potentially relevant boundaries at the outset. After preserving the original text, comparisons with quotes removed, comments deleted, or whitespace normalized can still be made; but each comparison should become a new sample and must not be written back as the original input.

Special floating-point forms were also treated as ordinary strings during this period. Someone would first replace one with a conventional numeric value to see whether the node could continue to appear. This often advanced the observation to the later node layer, but the replacement also changed lexical recognition and numeric interpretation. Even if an attribute subsequently appeared, that could not establish that the original form had been correctly accepted. The description on the old page, "normal after changing it to an ordinary number," could only show that the replacement text continued.

To avoid missing this detail, a side note required that an anomaly near lexical processing include at least the raw lexeme and the actual locale in the same record. Writing only "floating-point issue" was meaningless; writing only "it got better after changing the environment" was also meaningless. Both shorthand descriptions conflated the input, environment, and subsequent node observations.

## A Reproduction That Did Not Separate the Problem

Subsequent reproduction attempts changed only the locale, while the rest of the text remained unchanged. The result did not produce a clean separation: some texts still stopped near comments or whitespace, while others reached node reading and only then showed differences in attributes. That round of observation did not provide enough material to assign the cause to either branch.

This reproduction was later misread as two opposite conclusions. One claim was that "the locale had already been ruled out"; the other was that "the locale had already been confirmed as the sole factor." Both claims went beyond the records from that time. Switching the environment alone did not reliably separate the observed phenomena into purely lexical and purely attribute-related categories; it could only show that the condition change itself did not provide enough discrimination.

There was also a more practical gap in the reproduction: node snippets were not always obtained from the same input. Some checks first deleted comments, some first removed the quotes around names, and some first replaced special numeric values with ordinary numbers. The resulting node results could help locate the next place worth examining, but they could not be placed alongside the original anomaly for a causal assessment. The input had changed, so the node and attribute results represented another sample.

Therefore, later records split "node appears" into two questions: whether the node appears, and whether it comes from the unaltered original text. The former could only determine whether it was possible to temporarily switch to the attribute branch; the latter determined whether the node could be used to compare the original anomaly. The old page made no such distinction, causing many judgments that "the attributes had already been verified" to become impossible to trace back.

## 2024-02: The Split After On-Call Review

The on-call review changed the records to preserve the material first and decide the next step afterward. If there was no evidence that the node had formed, the issue was first handled under the lexical branch: save the text from the original image, the snippets before and after the anomaly, the actual locale, and the failed text. If the node already existed but the attribute results did not match expectations, the issue was handled under the attribute branch: save the node snippet and the attribute portion, and note whether these snippets came from the input as-is.

This does not split the problem into two unrelated implementation modules. A sample can be sensitive to lexical boundaries and can also exhibit attribute differences after a node is formed. The purpose of recording them separately is simply to avoid substituting a description from a later stage when the earlier stage has not been confirmed. Whether the text actually forms a node is the most useful stopping point during the current shift's troubleshooting.

"Attribute not read" is broken out into separate cases in this version. It may mean that the attribute is completely missing, that the attribute value does not meet expectations, or that reading was interrupted near the attribute. Without a node fragment, even these three cases are difficult to distinguish. Older records habitually wrote them as one sentence; after review, that sentence may no longer be used to directly infer the attribute name, default value, or read order.

The review also retained the previous cautious stance toward locale. The actual locale must be recorded together with the corresponding text; an environment note cannot be added afterward based on memory. When a failure occurs near a numeric form without environment information, it cannot be attributed to numeric semantics; when the behavior disappears after an environment change, that result cannot be used to overwrite the original failure. The environment is a test condition, not an explanation that is automatically valid.

## Retained Legacy Procedure

> Legacy procedure, now for historical reference only: first replace special floating-point notation with an ordinary number; if a node appears, investigate the attributes; if it still stops, adjust locale.

This procedure is no longer applicable. It treats "a node appears after replacement" as evidence that the original text passed the lexical stage, and "it still fails after replacement" as evidence that the environment has not been configured correctly. The former inference overlooks the fact that the input has changed; the latter overlooks the fact that the failure location has not yet been confirmed.

The legacy procedure was not deleted because it explains why later samples contain two similar but nonidentical texts: one retains the special floating-point term, while the other rewrites it as an ordinary numeric value. The two can be placed under the same event, but they cannot replace each other in the records. If only the rewritten sample remains later, it is only possible to say that the subsequent path was observed; a conclusion about the original-form text cannot be added retroactively.

Likewise, the old practice of first cleaning up comments and whitespace and then observing the attributes can still be used as a quick way to locate sensitive regions, but the result must be labeled as cleaned-up input. It cannot prove that lexical boundaries in the original text are irrelevant, nor can it prove that attribute reading is functioning normally for the original text.

## Review Limitations

The review did not require this page to be expanded into a description of all parser behavior. The current incident concerns only lexing and locale, quoted identifiers, comments, extra whitespace, special floating-point literals, and the boundary involving Node Attribute Reading. During troubleshooting, preserving these categories of input clues first is enough to avoid most conflated records; without evidence, there is no need to fill the gaps with a complete set of grammar rules.

The review also rejected another approach: first establish a baseline from formatted "normal text," then infer the original text from that baseline. Formatting specifically removes local conditions such as quotes, comment positions, and whitespace boundaries. Normal text can serve as an independent control, but it cannot replace the original failure sample, much less be called an equivalent copy of the abnormal input.

On-duty personnel must clearly distinguish between two stopping conditions. First, if the original text or actual locale is missing, or if it is impossible to confirm whether a node exists, stop at the lexical branch. Second, if the node fragment was not obtained from the unmodified input, or if there is no attribute section, stop at the attribute branch. Stopping does not mean that the anomaly has been ignored; it means that the existing records are insufficient to support a stronger attribution.

The principle left after review is narrowly scoped: change only one category of conditions per comparison. Removing quotes, deleting comments, normalizing whitespace, switching locale, replacing special numeric values, these are distinct actions. If multiple actions occur at the same time, the record can only state "a change was observed with the rewritten input", and cannot single out one action as the cause.

## On-site troubleshooting tree

The tree below preserves the original runbook purpose of this page. It does not describe the complete reading process, but specifies what to capture first when an anomaly occurs, when switching branches is allowed, and when to stop.

```text
An anomaly is found in the graph text, or in the node attribute results
│
├─ A. Node formation has not yet been confirmed
│  │
│  ├─ A1. The anomaly is near a quoted graph, input or output identifier
│  │  ├─ Save the name and the complete text before and after it
│  │  ├─ Do not remove the quotes first, or replace it with a shortened name first
│  │  └─ If the behavior changes after only removing quotes: save this as a comparison, and remain at the lexical boundary
│  │
│  ├─ A2. The anomaly is near comments or extra whitespace
│  │  ├─ Save the original passage including adjacent text
│  │  ├─ Use two separate comparisons for deleting comments and normalizing whitespace
│  │  └─ If both have already been changed at the same time: do not compare attributes, record that the input has been rewritten
│  │
│  ├─ A3. The anomaly is near a special floating-point literal
│  │  ├─ Save the original lexeme exactly as it is and the actual locale
│  │  ├─ Do not overwrite the original lexeme with an ordinary numeric value
│  │  └─ If the original lexeme cannot be preserved: do not judge whether that literal is accepted
│  │
│  └─ A4. The failure location is unclear
│     └─ First confirm whether any nodes have been constructed; if this cannot be confirmed do not move to B
│
└─ B. A node has been obtained, but the attribute results do not match expectations
   │
   ├─ B1. The node comes from the unmodified original text
   │  ├─ Save the node snippet and the attribute section
   │  ├─ Document missing attributes, abnormal values or interrupted reading separately
   │  └─ If material from A is also available, retain the link between their inputs
   │
   ├─ B2. The node comes from manually cleaned-up text
   │  ├─ Save it as a separate sample
   │  └─ Do not use it to explain the original text, return to A if necessary
   │
   └─ B3. There is only a description saying "attributes were not read"
      └─ Stop if the node snippet and attribute section are unavailable, do not guess attribute names
```

A and B are documentation branches, not guarantees about the internal layers of the code. The key question in A is whether the text has already produced a node; the key question in B is whether the node and the attribute section can be traced back to the same input. A sample may eventually move from A to B, but even if the final discussion concerns attributes, that does not justify erasing the original observations from stage A.

### Branch A: Preserve lexical boundaries first

When entering A, save the original graph text first, not a cleaned-up reproduction. The snippet must cover the identifiers, comments, whitespace and numeric regions near the anomaly. There is no need to create a separate neater example for the record here; real anomalies often occur precisely at boundaries that disappear during cleanup.

If the text contains quoted names, preserving the names themselves is not enough; also preserve the text immediately before and after them. A control with only the quotation marks removed can help determine whether the boundary is sensitive, but if that control passes, the only conclusion is that positions associated with quotation marks warrant further inspection. It does not automatically show that the locale is now correct, nor that the node attribute branch is irrelevant.

If comments are immediately adjacent to identifiers or numeric values, first preserve the comments in their original positions, then run another control with only the comments removed. If the behavior changes after removal, the original failing text should still remain in the record. The text after removal is not the "actual input," but an explicitly modified control. Whitespace cleanup follows the same principle: if processing can continue after whitespace is collapsed, this only shows that the boundary is sensitive to formatting, not which pair of adjacent lexemes caused the problem.

The locale must be recorded alongside that particular sample. Without environment information, do not infer numeric rules from errors near floating-point values; if processing can continue with the text after switching environments, do not overwrite the original anomaly either. A recurring misuse on the old page is to write "the locale was changed" as the final conclusion, when it is actually just a change in conditions.

If branch A cannot obtain the original text or locale, or cannot confirm whether the node has been constructed, stop at A. At this point, the most valuable material is not speculation about some attribute-reading behavior, but the complete text fragment and the actual failure location. When someone later obtains a new sample, they should also keep the new sample separate from the gaps in the old record, rather than use the new input to fill in details that were not recorded for the old input.

### Branch B: Nodes and attributes must come from the same input

Before entering B, first ask whether the node was obtained from unmodified text. If comments were deleted, quotation marks changed, whitespace collapsed, or numeric values replaced to allow reading to continue, that node can only represent the modified sample. It may still help with subsequent investigation, but it cannot be used to prove that attribute reading was already working correctly in the original anomaly.

In branch B, the focus of what is saved shifts to the node fragment and the attribute section. The record does not need to determine immediately whether the attribute problem belongs to lexing, reading, or subsequent interpretation; first record "the node exists" and "the attribute result does not match expectations" as two independent observations. Missing attributes, abnormal attribute values, and interrupted reading are different phenomena and must not all be shortened to "the attribute was not read."

Only if the same original text can show both the node appearing and the attribute anomaly can the two observations be compared side by side. Even then, do not immediately declare that the earlier lexical conditions are irrelevant. Lexical boundaries may determine the span of the subsequent node text; attribute reading occurs later. Whether the two are related must be supported by the same material; the issue title cannot serve as a substitute.

Branch B also has conservative stopping points: if there is no node fragment, no attribute section, or the input source has already changed, do not fill in missing attribute names, default behavior, or reading order. Older records added speculation here that could not later be checked against the original samples, so that practice is no longer followed.

## Current guidance near the end

The parser must accept quoted graph, input, and output identifiers, as well as comments and extra whitespace, and must still parse special floating-point literals such as inf according to the published syntax when the locale uses a comma as the decimal separator; the similar but invalid inf1 must still be rejected.

This requirement separates the old page's practices of "change the locale first" and "clean up the text first" from the syntax boundaries that must actually be upheld. For quoted names, comments, and extra whitespace, do not first delete or format them to obtain a superficial pass, then record the modified result as acceptance of the original text. For special floating-point literals, likewise do not first replace them with ordinary numbers to bypass reading and then claim that the syntax in its original form has been covered.

Currently, when valid text cannot be read any further, first return to branch A and save the input as-is and the locale. If a similar but invalid form is accepted, likewise retain the actual text and stop at the lexical branch; do not recast it as a node attribute event. Only after confirming that the node was constructed from unmodified text should you enter branch B to record the attribute behavior.

The current guidance here does not define all behavior after Node Attribute Reading. It only explains the adjacent public syntax boundaries relevant to this page and provides a way to categorize evidence during investigation without confusing lexical evidence with attribute evidence. `onnx/defs/parser.h` remains the starting point for cross-checking old records, but the path alone is not enough to trace all attribute behavior to the same location in the implementation.

## Related issues not yet split out

The user-facing entry point for Node Attribute Reading may still group several different situations under the same description: sometimes no node is formed at all, sometimes a node has been formed but its attribute section is incomplete, and sometimes the record contains only a result without a node snippet. The current material is insufficient to define uniform follow-up behavior for these cases, and they should not be forced into the lexical rules either.

One is the original graph text, the location of the anomaly, and the actual locale; the other is the node snippet and attribute section obtained from the same original graph text. If only one type can be provided, stop at the corresponding branch. Do not invent attribute results that never appeared just to make the record look complete.

This page also does not detail the specific call relationships between the old troubleshooting leads and the current entry point. The path is sufficient as a place to begin cross-checking, but the old issue name is not enough to prove that every attribute anomaly passes through the same location. This gap is left here to avoid presenting a navigation hint as a conclusion about the implementation.

## Retained appendices

### Appendix A: Quick cleanup method (deprecated)

When anomalies occurred in old samples, some people would first delete comments and excess whitespace, then remove the outer symbols around quoted names. If the text could then be read further, they attributed the remaining differences to attributes. This method was quick when organizing screenshots of failures, but it changed the input's lexical boundaries. It is now retained as a historical record and is no longer used to assess the original issue.

### Appendix B: Numeric substitution method (deprecated)

Another old method was to replace special floating-point text with ordinary numeric values to check whether a node could appear. It could help reveal whether there were other anomalies further along the path, but it could not prove that the original numeric text had been correctly recognized. The old page once described "the node appears after substitution" as successful reading; that conclusion was later withdrawn.

### Appendix C: Blank fields left by the old checklist

- Whether the input retained as-is preserved quotation marks, comments, and extra whitespace:
- Whether the actual locale was saved together with the text that failed:
- Whether the node was constructed from unmodified input:
- Whether the attribute snippet can be traced back to the same input:
- Whether the anomaly description refers to missing data, abnormal values, or interrupted reading:

These blank fields have not been filled in to create a unified process. They remain at the end because what old records most often lack is not a single-sentence conclusion, but the original material needed to determine which of the two branches, A or B, applies.

## Interface Decision

The public inlining interface is `onnx.inliner.inline_local_functions(model: ModelProto, convert_version: bool = False) -> ModelProto`. It returns a new model without modifying the input; it recursively inlines opset-compatible local functions and removes expanded definitions. The default False retains functions with a ONNX opset mismatch, along with their calls; True attempts to convert the function body from its ONNX opset to the model opset before inlining it, preserving the semantics of the converted graph (the legacy ReduceLogSum axes attribute becomes an input supplied by a Constant, and the original attribute is removed). The pairs in `inline_selected_functions(model, function_ids: list[tuple[str,str]], exclude: bool = False)` are domain/name; False expands selected functions, and True expands unselected functions. # Default Quantization Type Decision Record

This record remains in IR-18 Compatibility Window's old materials because "Default Quantization Type" still brings people back here. The original decision was narrow: initially treat an omitted type as a fixed value so that one node regression sample could retain a clear expected result. In retrospect, the real weakness was not whether the sample could run, but that this local judgment had been read as a broader type policy.

The original starting point for reading is still `onnx/backend/test/case/node/quantizelinear.py`. The direct dependencies visible in the file are `import numpy as np`, `import onnx`, `from onnx.backend.test.case.base import Base`, and `from onnx.backend.test.case.node import expect`. These clues point to the regression samples for QuantizeLinear; they do not list every place where models are constructed or explain how other quantization nodes handle omitted types.

## The decision built into the sample at the time

Window preparation required a decision that could be applied to the existing sample. The draft listed three options: set no default at all; treat all omitted types as errors; or take a default only from the node case at hand.

The first option would leave the expectation represented by `expect` for each call site to interpret. The second looked more conservative, but at the time there was no corresponding exception path, error text, or revised sample to support it. So the third option was adopted: **Default Quantization Type = UINT8.**

The original text also included `zero_point` in the same judgment. As long as a sample was near this group of quantization inputs, no distinction was made about where the omitted type came from. The benefit of this wording was that the regression sample could remain fixed; the problem was that whether the type was omitted, whether a zero point was present, and how quantized values were stored were three different issues. The draft did not separate them.

The option to "wait for confirmation from consumers before deciding" was not chosen at the time. That approach would suit a more complete migration review, but it could not answer what the sample in the window should expect that day. The old decision was therefore not a general type inference rule, but a temporary resolution for that sample; this scope limit was not always apparent when it was cited later.

## Review added later in the margin

This review did not infer implementation ownership from the file location; it only reconfirmed why this page had been retained as an entry point. `quantizelinear.py` shows node cases alongside `Base` and `expect`; that is enough to explain why the old judgment could be included in the regression materials, but not enough to fill in its full caller scope.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NodeCaseReading
    NodeCaseReading --> OldWindowPolicy
    OldWindowPolicy --> RollbackCheckRegistration
    RollbackCheckRegistration --> CurrentConsumerInventory
```

## Branches left incomplete

"Reject if the type is omitted" is still not the decision on this page. The old draft had no rejection behavior available for that path, so retroactively writing it in as the approach taken at the time would change the original record. Another reading would let the presence or absence of `zero_point` directly determine the default type; this was not written as a standalone rule either, but was only a blended judgment left by the draft's placing the two side by side.

The old judgment actually resolved a smaller problem: in the QuantizeLinear regression scenario at the time, tests did not have to be left without an expected result because of an omitted type. It did not address models with an omitted type but nothing corresponding to `zero_point`, nor did it confirm whether the node sample at hand could represent other quantization nodes. The inventory of current consumers is at ONX-206. This review will initially center on `onnx/version_converter/adapters/axes_input_to_attribute.h`. # opset attribute migration proposal

The scope remains the original class of axes migrations around `onnx/version_converter/adapters/axes_input_to_attribute.h`. This file is useful when tracing back from an old issue name, but the path alone does not show that the entire conversion happens here. The early draft focused on "whether attributes are lost"; review showed that we also need to look at which stage of the graph callers see once the attributes are in the target representation.

Retaining the old attributes has the advantage of fewer changes to the node layout during conversion. It is useful for first checking whether the original fields are still present, while deferring the question of what the target representation requires. The trade-off is that part of the graph will carry both the old attributes and the representation expected by the target. If subsequent processing does not recognize this mixed state, the problem will only resurface elsewhere.

Migrating directly to the target representation in the adapter looks cleaner. If the old model stores the set of axes in an attribute but the target requires an input in that position, the work involves at least: obtaining a usable value from the attribute, deciding whether to reuse an existing source for that value or add a new node, and then connecting it to the original node. Any of these steps may make the graph during conversion differ from the graph before conversion. Here, "the attribute names match" is not enough to claim that the semantics have been migrated.

## Verification leads

The public description for ONX-207 is "the public entry point currently supports opset Attribute Migration". This statement helps with the continuing search for the entry point, but does not specify which attributes are supported, which versions are covered, or whether consumers only read the final model or read the graph during conversion. A specific gap remains on the card: find a caller still using this migration and check the actual version, entry point, and current result.

Therefore, the existence of an entry point is only a starting point for a graph-level trial. Without the caller's version and results, a single local conversion cannot establish caller compatibility. The earlier assumption that "we can find the adapter" meant "we can go straight to choosing when to migrate" was premature.

## Samples to keep separate

axes can be recorded in at least three states: an explicit set, an explicitly empty set, and no attribute provided. An empty set is a value supplied by the model; a missing attribute means the model has not supplied this information. The available material does not show that these can follow the same migration branch across all operators or target opsets.

The trial record should first list the input model's opset, which state axes is in, and whether the graph already has an equivalent value source. For the output, record where the target representation is placed, whether the original attribute is retained, and whether any new nodes or new input dependencies appear. If the target form requires an input but no equivalent source can be found, the trial should stop here; a default value must not be used to disguise a missing attribute as an explicit set of axes.

## Trial scope

This trial will not expand to cover the entire version-conversion chain. A usable sample only needs to answer: what the set of axes represents before conversion, where it is represented after conversion, whether the added input changes node order, and whether the original model is modified. Reading the original model back through the old entry point can only check that the trial has not damaged the input; it does not mean that the old entry point should understand the conversion result.

If a caller only consumes the final model, earlier or later migration may not reveal a difference; if a caller inspects the intermediate graph, a new node, a change in input order, or how long the old attributes are retained could all be sources of differences. No caller of the second type has been found yet, so neither approach can be designated as the default on this page.

For Attribute Field Cleanup, DOC-21 can also be consulted, but that work will not be folded into this trial. Migration addresses where the old attributes' semantics go in the target representation; cleanup addresses when fields are removed. If both are changed at once and a difference appears, it will be impossible to tell whether it came from input construction, attribute retention, or field cleanup.
