# opset Attribute Migration Proposal

This record retains a section of an unresolved review in IR-18 Compatibility Window, not a completed migration description. It originally started from `onnx/version_converter/adapters/axes_input_to_attribute.h`, because the earlier investigation brought axes-related issues near this adapter. Only during later review was the concern over "whether the old attribute would disappear" split apart: one part concerns where the target representation is placed, and the other concerns who will see the change after a new input is added to the graph.

The file path remains a local verification entry point, not a conclusion about implementation ownership. It can help locate the old adapter and related objects, but it cannot prove that all version conversions pass through here, nor that callers see only the final model. The old draft once treated the path's proximity as a reason to migrate early; that is no longer being adopted.

## The Early Wording Remains Here

The first draft listed two routes. The first was to retain the old attribute at a later point in the conversion and have the target side or a later step process it. This results in fewer changes to the intermediate graph and makes it easier to confirm that the old attribute has not been discarded. The cost is that the old attribute form and the representation required by the target opset may coexist for a period, and later consumers must understand this transitional state.

The second was to switch to the target representation while the adapter processes the object. Its appeal is that downstream code receives the same form earlier and no longer needs to keep checking the old attribute. However, if the old model provides axes only as an attribute while the target form requires an input, migration is not just a matter of moving the field name to another position. An equivalent value must first be obtained, after which it must be determined whether that value comes from an existing node, whether a node must be constructed, and whether connecting the input will change the original dependency order.

The tendency at the time was to try the second route first, for a simple reason: if the axis set remains unchanged, unifying the representation earlier makes it easier to read. This old judgment was not deleted because it explains the starting point for the later trial; however, it did not distinguish consumers of the final model from consumers of the intermediate graph. The former may care only about the semantics after conversion, while the latter may observe differences caused by new nodes, input positions, or how long the old attribute remains. These two scenarios cannot be treated as the same result based only on "conversion succeeded."

Another old idea was that graph processing could continue as long as the graph structure did not go beyond the axes-related scope. That boundary is also too coarse. Some graph changes may be required by the target representation itself. What really requires stopping is not that "a change appears," but that the correspondence between the change and the old attribute's semantics cannot be explained.

## Looking Back from the Public Entry Point

The public description of ONX-207 says, "The current public entry point supports opset Attribute Migration." It provides a lead for continuing to look for callers and also shows that this discussion should not stop at a single header file. It does not list the attribute set, applicable version combinations, or the point at which the caller observes the graph; expanding this sentence into a complete compatibility commitment would be inappropriate.

The unfinished item left on the card is specific: find a caller that still uses this migration, and verify the actual version, entry point, and current result. The previous page turned "can find the entry point" into "can choose to migrate early," but that wording was later changed. The existence of an entry point only allows locating to begin; it cannot substitute for a caller sample. Without a version, entry point, and result, a graph-level trial also cannot be written up as caller compatibility.

This lead was later moved into an in-progress state, but that does not mean the sample has been completed. The current page has no caller name, actual version, or run result that can be recorded, so it still retains only candidate approaches. The next time someone follows ONX-207 to find a usage site, that usage's entry point and the graph phase it receives should be put back on this page, rather than deriving a conclusion from the card title.

## axes Must Not Be Conflated into One Kind of Input

During the review, the old draft listed empty axes and missing axes in the same column. They are now divided into three states:

- Explicit axes: the model provides concrete axis values;
- Empty axes: the model explicitly provides an empty set;
- Missing axes: the model does not provide this attribute.

An empty set is not "no information," and a missing attribute is not "another way to write an empty set." This page contains no evidence that these three states produce the same migration result for all operators and target opsets. A sample containing only non-empty axes can speak only to the specific set in that sample; it cannot be used to infer that an empty set and a missing attribute can be filled with the same default input.

Defaults require particular caution. A default may allow graph construction to continue, but it may also disguise an attribute that was originally missing as an explicitly provided axis set. If a difference appears after conversion, the opportunity to determine whether it came from the old model, input construction, or the caller's reading method is lost. The trial should first record the attribute state, and then determine whether an equivalent source can be connected to the target location.

An "equivalent source" does not require creating a new branch for every model. It only requires first clarifying what value the target form actually needs. If an existing node can express the same axis set, its meaning must still be checked when it is reused; if there is no source, a value must not be forced in merely to complete the conversion. This stopping point is more useful than asking whether the model reported an error, because the latter only means that the current path did not stop.

## What This Proposal Actually Tests

The proposal recommends a small, traceable trial, not a batch attribute cleanup. The sample should make the opset it uses and the source of axes apparent from the model. At the start, do not mix in other attributes or expand to multiple graph structures; otherwise, when a difference appears after conversion, it will be impossible to distinguish whether it was caused by attribute migration, node construction, or another transformation.

The record can be brief, but it should retain at least the following four areas:

| Location | Content to record |
| --- | --- |
| Before conversion | opset; whether axes is an explicit value, empty, or missing; whether the graph already has a reusable value source |
| After conversion | where the target representation resides; whether the old attribute is retained; whether extra nodes or input dependencies were added |
| Usage site | the actual entry point; whether it receives the original model, final model, or graph during conversion |
| Difference location | the first place where an inconsistency in the axis set, node order, or input source is observed |

The "usage site" row is still empty for now and should not be filled with an assumed caller. Without a usage site, the trial can be saved as a graph-level observation, but it must be kept separate from the compatibility assessment. Being able to read the old model back only checks that the trial did not rewrite the input model; it does not mean that the old entry point needs to understand the target model, nor that the target model preserves the same behavior for all old callers.

For the direct-migration route, the action should be divided into two steps. First confirm whether the corresponding position in the target opset can still be represented by an attribute; only when it cannot be carried by an attribute should construction of an input be discussed. After constructing the input, compare it against the axis set expressed by the original attribute. If the value comes from a new node, check the node insertion point and input order; if it comes from an existing node, check that reuse has not caused the existing node to take on a different meaning.

This does not require every adapter to use the same process; it is a local check for this axes trial. It arises from the different locations where the old attribute and the target input are carried, and should not be expanded into a universal statement about all attribute migrations.

## Where Each Route Loses Its Basis

The route of retaining the old attribute is not automatically justified merely because it makes fewer graph changes. Usage sites that consume only the final model may be able to isolate this deferral more easily; usage sites that read the intermediate graph may need to observe how long the old representation remains. There is currently no material for choosing between these two scenarios. Even if the final model can be loaded, that is not enough to conclude that early and late migration are equivalent for usage sites.

The direct-migration route also cannot be adopted simply because the target representation is tidier. When the target form requires an input but no equivalent source can be found, the trial should stop. If a new node changes the input order, first confirm whether any usage site reads that phase; if this information is unavailable, the change may only be recorded, not declared harmless.

The conditions for withdrawal or pausing are now more specific: when the correspondence between axes before and after conversion cannot be explained clearly, do not expand the sample; when the target location requires an input and there is no equivalent source, do not fill in a default value; when the node layout on which a usage site depends changes, first confirm which phase of the graph it reads; when the trial rewrites the original model, stop and save the original model and conversion result separately. The last item comes from the earliest concern that the input might be rewritten accidentally and must not be conflated with a backward-compatibility assessment.

If the difference appears only in the final model, first check the axis set and input source, then determine whether it is merely a change in representation location. If the difference has already appeared in the intermediate graph, the timing of the read itself becomes part of the trial. Without an actual entry point and version, it is not possible to choose on the caller's behalf whether migration should happen early or late.

## Separate from Attribute Field Cleanup

DOC-21 can continue to be used to inspect Attribute Field Cleanup, but it should not be treated as a follow-up step for this migration. Migration concerns how the semantics of the old attribute are preserved in the target representation; cleanup concerns when the field should be removed. The two changes may be near the same object, or they may have no shared call path. If they are tied together in one trial, then after a failure it will be impossible to attribute it to input construction, retention of the old attribute, or field removal.

Therefore, `axes_input_to_attribute.h` remains the local entry point for the old investigation. If it is later confirmed that a caller or another adapter participates in graph construction, the record should be updated according to the actual reference relationships, rather than continuing to infer from the filename. This page retains the two early routes and the later narrowing; it does not turn them into a current default migration rule.

There is currently no material selecting early or late migration, and no caller sample that can be recorded on this page. The next supplement should first specify one usage site's actual version, entry point, which graph phase it observes, and the result after conversion; if this information still cannot be found, the candidate status should be retained.

# Attribute Field Cleanup Troubleshooting Tree

## First, remember what the symptom looks like

This page does not address every attribute issue; it follows only the local troubleshooting path left by "Attribute Field Cleanup". The earliest records start with the issue name and call name and ultimately land on `onnx/defs/schema.h`. This landing point remains useful, but it can easily cause people to misread "the file that was indexed" as "the file that performs the cleanup." The actual verification entry is fixed at the `v_prev` revision of `internal/onnx-core`; that revision provides only local declarations within the file and adjacent navigation.

When the same symptom occurs, first preserve these three things verbatim: the attribute name used in the issue, the field spellings that appeared, and the call name that brought the investigation here. Do not first combine them into a "schema issue," and do not leave only a module name. Attribute Field Cleanup may simply be a way of describing the issue; you cannot infer from these few words that the cleanup action has already occurred near the declaration.

## Why the old record is still here

v1 knew only the path entry, not whether that entry could explain the full symptom. At the time, it treated `onnx/defs/schema.h` as the first checkpoint, which was a reasonable working assumption; but a file match by itself provides no evidence that the attribute was deleted, retained, or migrated.

Subsequent maintenance confirmed that the issue name and call name still lead people to this file, so the old entry cannot be removed. What needs to be corrected is how it is used: first check the local content at the revision containing the path, then decide whether to continue tracing references. Keep the old "start looking here," but do not keep the old "this is the processing point."

## Entry and record format

The fixed verification entry is as follows:

- Repository: `internal/onnx-core`
- Version: `v_prev`
- Path: `onnx/defs/schema.h`
- Current match terms: `interop`, `float`, `attributeproto`

These four items fix the review scope to a single file artifact. Match terms are only indexing clues; even when all three hit the same location, that does not mean they belong to the same field cleanup. At each hit, record at least these local facts:

- Whether the matched object is a declaration, type name, comment, or adjacent name;
- Whether the attribute name and field name appear there verbatim;
- Whether the call name appears directly in the file contents or was brought in by the old record;
- Whether a local relationship was found that can lead onward to the referring party.

Without these distinctions, the result is merely a "found it" record and cannot be used to attribute the cleanup.

## Troubleshooting Tree

```text
An anomaly related to Attribute Field Cleanup is observed
├─ Can the original property names, field names and call names be retained?
│  ├─ No: Stop at organizing the input for now, without substituting generic terms for fields
│  └─ Yes: Proceed to local verification of schema.h
├─ Is there a match in schema.h at the specified revision?
│  ├─ No: Retain the path entry point and record that no match was found; do not replace it with a guess based on the current working tree
│  └─ Yes: Distinguish the match type
│      ├─ Only declarations or type names: Continue looking for direct references
│      ├─ Adjacent property descriptions exist: Record the adjacency, without determining the execution location
│      └─ The call name also appears: Compare it word for word with the original observation
└─ Has a reference that can be linked to the cleanup action been found?
   ├─ Yes: Record the referenced object and the fields it changes
   └─ No: Stop at local declarations, leaving items pending verification
```

The purpose of this tree is to separate "path matches", "adjacency relationships" and "actual field changes". If evidence is missing at any level, do not jump to a definitive conclusion at the next level.

## Branch One: The original fields can be reproduced

If the observation record still retains the property names and field spellings, first look for the corresponding text in `onnx/defs/schema.h`, then check the three frozen match terms individually. When a property name is found, record which declaration it is adjacent to; when it is not found, do not treat a similar `float` or `attributeproto` as a field with the same name.

If the three match terms only identify different adjacent locations, document the locations separately. One location may contain only a type declaration, while another may contain only a name near an interface. They can help with tracing back together, but they must not be combined in the record into "this is responsible for cleaning up properties".

If a direct reference is visible, put the referenced object, the fields read and the fields that change in the same record. Only when all three line up can the path be advanced from an index entry point to a behavior entry point. If field changes are still not visible, retain "Local declaration matched, cleanup action not verified".

## Branch Two: Only a call name is available, with no field name

A call name is not enough to prove where property cleanup occurs. First return to the record that produced the anomaly, and confirm whether the call name is the original text and whether it was relayed by a previous investigator. If the field spelling cannot be recovered, `onnx/defs/schema.h` may be retained as an entry point, but stop attributing the behavior to the implementation.

In this branch, do not use any of the terms `interop`, `float` or `attributeproto` to replace the missing field. They are match terms already present in the current index, not aliases for the field in question. Once the original field is obtained later, start again from Branch One.

If the call name can be found near the file, but there is no corresponding property name, record "Call-name adjacency observed, field relationship not observed". This is more useful than documenting adjacent declarations as cleanup logic, because the next review can continue directly from the missing relationship without having to locate the path again.

## Branch Three: Only property-related declarations are matched

When a search matches a declaration, first confirm which local object it belongs to, then check whether there are any direct references. Do not infer from the declaration's name that it deletes, renames, or retains properties. For this page, the minimum confirmable finding is: the file at the specified revision contains a local declaration or adjacent object related to the matched term.

If the current material directly identifies the referencing code, record the three-part relationship "declaration—reference—field change". If only the relationship between the declaration and an adjacent object is visible, record it only as far as that adjacent object. If an older record claims that this is the processing location, but no corresponding reference can be found in this check, retain the old claim as a historical lead while making clear that it has not been confirmed by the current local material.

Do not invent a nonexistent caller just to complete a branch of the tree. When there is no caller, the stopping condition is "declaration located, execution relationship unconfirmed". This is not a troubleshooting failure, but the limit of the evidence for that revision.

## Branch four: Search results do not match the observed behavior

If `schema.h` does not contain the original property name, or the matched term appears only in adjacent declarations unrelated to the observed behavior, first confirm that you are checking `v_prev`, then confirm that the path has not been changed to a different file. If both the version and path are correct but the results still do not match, retain the original troubleshooting entry point and state "the observed behavior has not been linked to the local declaration".

Do not directly overwrite this result with the contents of the current working tree. The current working tree may change where matches occur and may make older records look more complete, but it cannot clarify the relationships involved in the historical issue in `v_prev`. When a comparison is needed, record the two versions separately; do not retroactively record matches from the newer version as facts about the older version.

If the reviewer can provide only the issue name and call name, without fields or references within the file, stop at verifying the entry point. When handing off responsibility, include the original term, matched term, repository, version, and path to avoid starting the next round from a generalized "property issue" again.

## What to do after a failure

"Recovery" here does not mean arbitrarily modifying properties or deleting fields. Before the execution location is confirmed, do not test a hypothesis by changing schema declarations, changing property names, or deleting adjacent fields. Such actions change the object being investigated and cannot establish which layer produced the original anomaly.

If a review yields only a declaration match, the next step is not to expand the search to the entire project, but to find the missing direct references. If a review yields only a call name, the next step is to recover the original fields and observed behavior. If the versions do not match, first document the version differences, then reassess the search results. If there is insufficient material in all three cases, stop, and do not fill the gap with a broader conclusion.

There is also value in retaining unsuccessful investigation approaches: for example, "entered the file via the call name, but did not find a field relationship". This shows that the entry point is usable and that attribution is not yet complete. If this failed attempt is deleted from the record, the next maintainer will mistakenly think that the path has never been checked.

## revision, environment, and local results

This page references a fixed combination of repository, version, and path. Different working trees, different revisions, or renamed files may all produce different search results for `interop`, `float`, and `attributeproto`. When recording environment differences, include only differences that can be confirmed: repository name, revision, path, matched term, and the object observed.

Do not treat search results in the editor as behavioral outcomes. Search results can show where the text is, but cannot show whether the attribute fields have already been cleaned up. Do not treat descriptions of paths in old troubleshooting records as current reference relationships either; they can only explain why this file entry point was retained.

If further checks of upstream references are needed, the handoff should include: the original symptom, attribute name, field name, call name, file path, revision, the match results for each of the three search terms, and the condition at which the investigation is currently paused. If any item is missing, the next person taking over may have no choice but to repeat the path search.

## Responsibility Boundaries

For the interpretation of local schema declarations and reference relationships, defer to a maintainer who can directly inspect the revision corresponding to `onnx-core`. The meaning of the attribute in the public interface is to be confirmed by the public interface owner; the regression symptoms, version, and CI results are to be confirmed by the quality owner. Only local objects that have already been observed are recorded here, without filling in unobserved call edges on behalf of any party.

When the issue also involves caller compatibility, confirmed field changes can be passed on for further checks during joint debugging with the caller, but do not write the caller's assumptions back into the local facts for `schema.h`. Only after returning to the same revision and seeing the corresponding references should the attribution on this page be updated.

## Maintenance Side Notes

ONX-208 is the navigation entry point for the "Attribute Field Cleanup" investigation. It later entered the processing stage, showing that this material is still in use; card actions themselves do not show relationships within the file, so status changes cannot replace verification results.

This page and the material for Strict Error Propagation cover related issues, but do not merge the two investigations. The current page covers only the entry point, local declarations, reference checks, and stopping conditions for Attribute Field Cleanup. When you see another issue name, retain it as a routing clue and return to the respective materials.

If the latest review confirmed only the entry point and did not confirm the field changes, the version record should explicitly state "The entry point has been retained, and the relationships still await verification". If direct references were confirmed, add the specific objects and fields, without rewriting the earlier historical paragraphs. Keep the old working hypothesis at its chronological position in v1, and append new evidence only here.

## Checks Before Closure

- Whether the original property names, field names, and call names can still be reviewed;
- Whether the repository is `internal/onnx-core`, and the revision is `v_prev`;
- Whether the path is `onnx/defs/schema.h`;
- Whether hits for `interop`, `float`, and `attributeproto` are recorded separately;
- Whether declarations, adjacency, and direct references are kept separate;
- Whether a path entry point has been mistakenly recorded as an execution location;
- Whether, when there are no references, the record stops at a clearly identified gap rather than inventing a caller;
- Whether version differences are stored separately from historical material.

Meeting these conditions only means that the record of this investigation can be reviewed. It does not turn unseen cleanup actions into known facts, nor does it prejudge the next reference check.

## Boundaries of the sample record

This page can capture paths, terms, and local relationships, but each type of material has a different evidentiary scope. The issue name explains why the file was opened for this investigation; property names and field names indicate what must be preserved in the text; call names indicate the direction from which the old record was approached. Even when they appear together, they cannot be directly combined into "cleanup takes place here". Only when declarations, references, and field changes are visible in the same material is there reason to move the inspection point toward the entry point for the behavior.

Search results must be retained as they are, rather than first organized into a conclusion. For each hit, record at least the file path, revision, matched term, matched object, and whether the investigation can proceed to the next step as separate items. If two terms occur in different locations, mark them separately; if a term appears only in a comment or an adjacent name, faithfully record it as adjacency as well. Such records may look more fragmented than a single overall assessment, but they allow the next reviewer to determine which relationships have already been examined and which are merely similar names.

When encountering objects with similar field names, first preserve the original spelling, then check whether the object belongs to the same record as the original symptom. You must not replace a missing field with a broader term, nor claim that a property has already been handled merely because `float`, `interop`, or `attributeproto` appears in the file. Matching terms serve to narrow the reading scope; they have no authority to turn a declaration into an execution point.

## Comparing two revisions

When comparing old records with new material, first save the two sides in separate columns. Put only the old issue name, old path, and hits recorded at the time on the left; put the file, version, and local objects currently being viewed on the right. Identical paths do not mean identical content, and different paths do not mean the old record is no longer valid. If the current version contains an additional declaration that appears relevant, first state that it appears on the right; you must not retroactively attribute it to the time of the old record.

A comparison must answer at least three small questions: whether the old path can still be reproduced today; whether the existing hits actually connect to a reference; whether observable field changes appear at the reference site. The three answers may differ. For example, the path may still open, but only declarations are visible; or a reference may be found, yet no field change is visible. Recording these asymmetric results makes it easier to continue next time than collapsing all three into "confirmed".

If search outputs need to be saved side by side, retain filenames and the context around each match, and do not treat the editor-filtered summary as the complete material. Context is only for determining adjacency and cannot substitute for the actual call site. If no call site is currently available, explicitly write "Entry point reproduced, call unverified", and limit the next step to finding one real reference, without expanding the search to the entire repository.

## Minimum materials for handoff

When handing this investigation over to someone else, the handoff package should start with a specific sample, not a module name. Alongside the sample, include the original symptoms, attribute name, field name, call name, repository, revision, path, and the match locations for each search term; if material for any item is unavailable, mark it as not collected. This lets the person taking over first reproduce the existing entry point, then decide whether the gap concerns field relationships, reference relationships, or caller results.

Do not preselect an implementation file in the handoff, and do not use a card's state in place of a sample. ONX-208 only provides navigation; the state it enters cannot prove what kind of change occurred in `schema.h`. If the person taking over can obtain only a path, they should treat that path as a completed lookup step and continue looking for references, rather than jumping from "location complete" to "behavior confirmed".

When the same issue has multiple samples, record the object observed and the stopping point for each sample separately. One sample matches a declaration and another matches a call; the two can provide clues for each other, but cannot automatically be combined into a single causal chain. Group them under one relationship only after returning to the same revision to verify the intermediate references.

## How to preserve the investigation state when verification is paused

When the investigation pauses, retain the last reproducible entry point and the first result that did not match. Do not delete unsuccessful search approaches, and do not rewrite "not found" as "this object does not exist". The former tells those who come later how far the search got, while the latter can mislead them into thinking the object has already been ruled out. If a verification pass yields only a name, record the name and file location; if it yields a reference but no field change, record the reference and the missing change; if it yields a result but the entry point cannot be found, conversely, mark the result's source as still awaiting verification.

Follow the same sequence when restoring an old path. First confirm that the old path and old terms can still be reviewed, then check whether the newly added entry point ever had a real sample, and finally compare the caller results. When retracting an overly broad attribution, retract only the attribution text, retaining the time and materials from when it "was previously checked". This way, the next round will neither repeat the same search nor treat a failed attribution as a new fact.

The stopping points on this page are always the boundaries of the evidence: if you see a path, stop at the path; if you see a declaration, stop at the declaration; only when you see a direct reference should you proceed to checking field changes. If new material becomes available later, append it after the corresponding stopping point and indicate which revision it comes from. Earlier historical records must not be overwritten when new material appears; new material must not retroactively add relationships to old records that were not available at the time.

## Item-by-item checks of the handoff record

Before handoff, split each sample into four columns: entry-point file and revision, actual matches, reproducible direct references, and changes still awaiting verification. Put them on the same row only when all four columns come from the same search; when only the entry point and matches are available, explicitly write "unverified" in the last two columns, and do not fill them in using adjacent files. If the revision changes, keep the old row in its original position, start a new row, and state the differences.

For field cleanup, it is especially important to retain counterexamples. Seeing an attribute declared does not mean it has been removed from the output; seeing one successful serialization also does not mean that rerunning after a failure will clear temporary state. Reviewers should separately save the observable results of success, rejection, and a subsequent invocation, and identify which case still lacks evidence from an actual run. This lets the next person taking over continue from the gaps rather than mistake a navigation pointer for a conclusion about the implementation.

# Strict Error Propagation Migration Notes

This page initially contained only a filename and two search terms. After review, `onnx/defs/shape_inference.h` remains a historical reference point, but is no longer described as the sole home of Strict Error Propagation. The old record answered "where to start looking", not "at which layer the error is generated and propagated to the caller". These two questions must be kept separate, or later readers may easily mistake the reference location for an implementation entry point whose migration is already complete, simply because the directory has not changed.

The earlier investigation started from the issue name "Strict Error Propagation" and used `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror` to find this header file. Keeping these unchanged here serves a practical purpose: the issue name identifies the behavior being checked at the time, the search terms identify the local sections that were opened, and the file path preserves the location to revisit. If any of the three is missing, later readers will have to guess again why the old record stopped here.

## What the Old Entry Point Means

`onnx/defs/shape_inference.h` is the old reference path, not an automatically derived new path. The old record relates to the existing material for `internal/onnx-core`; at the time, the file was accessed using the issue name and call name, and only declarations and their adjacent context were visible. The filename alone cannot establish that the error originates in shape inference, nor can it establish that the caller depends directly on this file. The migration record should preserve this limited scope, rather than add an execution chain to the old record that was never found.

The old entry point therefore retains two uses. The first is to revisit the declaration scope containing `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror`, to confirm whether the new search still starts from the same objects. The second is to place failure output obtained later alongside the old record for comparison: did the old record merely match a name, or did it already point to a location that could explain the output. Both uses require the path to remain available, but neither requires describing that path as a conclusion about behavior.

The old entry point does not serve a third purpose: it cannot replace a real call. Without the call site, we do not know how `strict_mode` enters the current scenario; without the result visible to the caller Fang Ke, we do not know whether `inferenceerror` is the error seen by the user; without the runtime environment, we cannot tell whether a failure to reproduce is due to a change in the path, the input, or the environment. The old file can still be opened, but the fact that it can be opened is not grounds for declaring the migration complete.

## First Clarify What Is Being Migrated

What is being migrated here is not the header file, nor is it a matter of replacing one search term with another. What is being migrated is an investigation and verification path: starting from the old issue name, passing through a declaration location that can be revisited, and finally reaching a strict-mode call that can be rechecked. The new path is established only after that call has been recorded.

When recording the new path, at least the following must be kept together in one place:

- The original issue name that prompted the check;
- The actual entry location of the call;
- Whether any wrapping or conversion occurs before the call;
- How strict mode comes into play in this call;
- Where the error becomes the result visible to the caller Fang Ke;
- What role the old path still plays in the comparison.

This does not require filling in a complete call graph first. The current material provides neither a complete call graph nor a sample that can be rerun directly. This sequence is only intended to prevent "found the declaration" from being incorrectly recorded as "found the user entry point". If only one of these items has been confirmed, record only that item and leave the others unfilled.

The old record places `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror` together because they jointly formed the original search scope; the material on this page has not confirmed the specific control relationship between them. During subsequent reviews, do not interpret one as a switch and the other as the final error merely because their names appear next to each other. First record which declarations each appears near, then use a real call to establish whether both participate in the same path at the same time.

## Sequence for Moving Away from the Old Path

First, open the old path and record the local declarations currently visible and the immediate surroundings of the two search terms. The output of this step should be a description of a location that can be revisited, not an architecture diagram filled in based on the directory hierarchy. If `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror` have no direct relationship within the current view, record that accurately as well; this will prevent later records from combining two independent matches into a definitive conclusion.

The second step is to find a real call. What needs to be recorded is not an abstract statement that "strict mode is used somewhere", but where this call comes from, what context is passed in, whether it goes through wrapping first, and how the result it returns or throws reaches the caller. This page currently has no such call sample, so this step remains empty. Until a sample is found, names in the header file cannot stand in for the way the call is made.

Only in the third step should the old record and the new path be compared. First ask whether the old path still explains the declaration location in the new material; then ask whether the new call actually passes through that location; finally ask whether the result seen by the caller is the same as the error originally being checked. The answers to these three questions may differ. For example, the new call may still use the same declaration scope but expose the error to the caller through different wrapping; alternatively, the old path may retain only its search value, with the new call not passing through it at all. The migration record needs to accommodate both outcomes.

Only in the fourth step should the caller documentation be changed. There is currently no frozen caller list and no migration batch that can be confirmed, so this page must not invent callers that have already switched. Once a call is obtained, first attach it to the new path as an individual sample; group calls into a batch only after multiple calls have been confirmed one by one. A batch is a recording unit used later when organizing callers, not a label for filling the current gaps.

```text
Old issue name
   |
   +-- `strict_mode` / `inferenceerror`
   |          |
   |          v
   |   onnx/defs/shape_inference.h
   |          |
   |          +-- Declarations and adjacent context: can be revisited
   |
   +-- Real strict-mode call: to be added
                  |
                  +-- Wrapper location: to be added
                  +-- Caller result: to be added
```

The "to be added" labels in the diagram are not candidate module names. They indicate that the old record did not preserve enough material to fill in those nodes. When adding nodes later, start from an actual call and fill in both directions: upward with the call's origin, and downward with the result seen by the caller. Do not start guessing from neighboring directories or similarly named files, because that would turn navigation information back into an attribution judgment.

## Comparisons to Retain During Review

The old path, the new call, and the error result should be included in the same comparison, but they do not need to be presented as a continuous causal chain. The recommended recording method is to write down the old reference point first, then the call sample, and finally paste in the caller result; distinguish the three using "confirmed" and "not yet confirmed". This way, even if the new call is later shown to belong to another layer, the old record's value in identifying the declaration location will not be damaged.

The original issue name is the easiest thing to lose in the comparison. Later readers will often search directly for `strict_mode` or `inferenceerror`, then treat the search results as the issue itself. The original issue name should remain at the start of the record because it establishes that this check concerns Strict Error Propagation, not every location containing these two strings. Search terms can expand the search scope, but cannot replace the issue scope.

The second thing that is easy to lose is the context of the old revision. The old path comes from existing records, and the version of the material on which it was based should be retained when reviewing it, to avoid automatically projecting adjacent content in the current tree back onto the old conclusion. This does not require creating a new version note for every browsing session; simply noting beside the new call whether it and the old reference point come from the same material is enough to let later readers know that the two sides of the comparison are not inherently the same.

The third thing that is easy to lose is the result seen by the caller. The error name, exception object, and user-facing text may not be the same thing. This page currently preserves no specific output, so it cannot prescribe in advance what the result should look like. When adding samples, raw results take precedence over an edited summary; if only a summary is available, make clear that it establishes only that someone observed the issue, not the layer at which the error first appeared.

## Counterexamples and Stopping Points

After finding a candidate call, do not immediately describe it as the new entry point. At least two cases need to be distinguished: calls that enter strict mode but do not produce the error being checked, and calls that enter the same kind of scenario and do produce that error. Neither type of input is provided here, so regression samples must not be fabricated; however, the record template should reserve an item for each, to avoid treating every strict-mode call as the target entry point based solely on the failing side.

The value of counterexamples lies in narrowing attribution. If a call completes normally in strict mode, it at least reminds us that the name "strict mode" cannot explain the error on its own. If another call produces an error but has an additional wrapper layer in its path, the difference still cannot be attributed directly to the header file. First examine the locations each call passes through, then decide which difference is worth pursuing further.

When there is no comparable counterexample, the migration can stop at "candidate call found". This state is more useful than "migration complete" because it tells the next review what to bring back: a call that can fail, a call for comparison, and each call's path to the caller-visible result. Do not mark inputs that have not been run as passed or failed just to complete the table.

If the new call establishes only the entry location without explaining the error result, record "call located, propagation unverified". If only the error result is available, without a reliable call site, record "result collected, entry point unverified". If both are available but it remains unclear whether strict mode actually participates, record "call and result collected, mode relationship unverified". These states can coexist across different samples and should not be compressed into a single generic completion level.

## While the Old and New Paths Run in Parallel

Do not delete the historical reference path `onnx/defs/shape_inference.h` during the migration. Once a new entry point is found, add it as a new paragraph after the old path and state clearly whether it is a call entry point, a wrapper location, or an observation point for the caller result. Readers can then still return from the old issue name to the earliest declaration location, while also following the added material to see how far the later additions have progressed.

If the new entry point and the old path ultimately point to the same place, retain both names: the old path explains how it was found at the time, while the new entry point explains how its participation in the call was later verified. If they are no longer the same, there is still no need to delete the old path; note beside it that it is used only for historical comparison, and identify the new actual call separately. Deleting the old path would lead later readers to believe that the early record never existed, while retaining it without distinguishing its purpose would cause the opposite misreading.

Changes to the caller documentation should come after this step. There is currently no caller set available to record, so this page specifies only the recording sequence: first confirm an individual call, then confirm whether it represents a class of callers, and only then revise the caller-facing migration notes. If the notes are changed before the call is added, unverifiable claims that callers have "switched" can easily appear in the notes.

For experimental material related to Metadata Boundaries, see [DOC-23](DOC-23). It can help readers locate another record in the same compatibility window, but cannot supply call samples for Strict Error Propagation on this page. Keep the inputs, results, and conclusions of the two records separate, to avoid mixing unrecorded observations merely because the topics are related.

## How to Restore the Old Path

Restoring does not mean erasing all newly added content. If the new entry point later fails to reproduce the old issue, first withdraw the description identifying it as the migration target, while retaining the record that the entry point was examined and the results obtained at the time. Keep the old reference path, the original issue name, `strict_mode`, and `inferenceerror`, because they are the starting points for locating it again next time.

After restoring, recheck in the original order: whether the old path's local declarations can still be revisited; whether the new call was actually recorded; whether the caller result comes from that same call; whether strict mode is merely a search clue or has been shown by a sample to participate. These checks do not require explaining the entire module again, but prevent an incorrect attribution from leaving behind text that is harder to deal with than the original gap.

If the new material changed only the reference location, without changing the caller documentation, restoring requires only withdrawing the attribution judgment about the new location. If the caller documentation already references the new entry point, first change it back to "call sample pending verification", then remove statements such as "migration complete". The old file path should not be used as a rollback target for replacing code; this page preserves investigation paths and relationships between materials, not code modification instructions.

After restoring, a brief explanation of the failure reason is enough, such as "the candidate call could not be matched to the original result" or "the wrapper location has not yet been confirmed". Do not rewrite a single unmatched sample into a new overall conclusion. It only indicates that the sample cannot currently serve as the migration entry point, and it may still provide a comparison for the next search.

## Evidence Still Needed from Actual Usage

The current gaps are concentrated in the following items:

- The most recent real call and its entry location;
- Whether the call goes through wrapping or conversion;
- The raw error result seen by the caller;
- The version and runtime environment associated with that result;
- A strict-mode counterexample that can be distinguished from the failing call;
- Whether an actual reference relationship exists between the old reference point and the new call;
- Whether enough callers have been confirmed to form a migration batch.

Until this material is available, `onnx/defs/shape_inference.h` remains a useful historical entry point, and `strict_mode` and `inferenceerror` remain usable search points; none of them constitutes evidence that the migration of Strict Error Propagation is complete. The next addition to the record should start from a real call and append the newly obtained content after the existing path on this page.

versions.body:
# Leaf Link Trial Proposal

In IR-18 Compatibility Window, Leaf Link is called out separately because its handling cannot be combined with parent-directory handling into a single path rule. Here, "final" refers only to the last path component corresponding to the external data filename; whether parent directories traverse links is not being settled in this interface review.

The initial view is to put the check near the interface that opens external data, rather than having each reader interpret paths on its own. The aim isn't to restructure all external-data flows. The concern is simply that once a caller handles a link ahead of time, the later open operation can no longer see the original boundary.

There are two candidate approaches.

- The reader first checks the supplied path text, then decides whether to proceed with opening it.
- Retain the final-component object in the helper interface responsible for opening external data, and have that interface accept or reject it.

The first looks like a smaller change, but the same model could get different decisions at different call sites. The second requires first confirming whether the interface can cover the existing read paths, but it centralizes the decision and makes it easier to keep regression samples in one place.

The recommendation for this round is to try only the second approach. The trial does not require addressing Parent Directory Link first, and does not switch Regular External File to a different set of entry points. Prepare one Regular External File and one sample whose final component is a link, and check each to see whether opening still happens in the same helper layer.

Still undecided: the form of the response returned to the caller on rejection; whether reading and saving share the same boundary; and who should interpret an ordinary path that contains a link name but whose final component is not a link. If the trial forces callers to reconstruct paths themselves, set aside the idea of consolidating the interfaces and keep the existing read paths.

# Leaf Link Final-Component Link Trial Proposal

This was initially framed as a small API issue: when an external data path reaches its final component, should the caller first determine whether it is a link? That framing turned out to be insufficient. The caller sees a string; the open operation sees an object. If resolution has already happened between the two, the final-component boundary can easily be erased too early.

However, Leaf Link isn't synonymous with the entire path-safety policy either. This proposal covers only the final path component of external data files within the model directory. Parent directories traversed through links, legacy behavior for ordinary directory links, and cases where the caller has proactively expanded the path are not covered by the rules here. Parent-directory handling remains tracked separately by DOC-26, so the same sample is not independently interpreted on two pages.

## Direction retained from the initial draft

The initial draft proposed that the reader check the supplied path before entering the helper layer. The immediate benefit was clear: changes would be concentrated at a small number of call sites, and failures could return earlier. It remains here because it shows why the review initially leaned toward a text-based check.

But this recommendation is no longer the subject of the trial. Path text can express only the name passed in by the caller; it cannot stand in for checking the final object. If each reader writes its own check, Leaf Link becomes a caller convention rather than a boundary of the external-data interface. This issue usually does not show up in ordinary-file samples; only link samples can expose it.

The draft also included the line "All links are handled by the same interface." That line is deprecated. It conflated the directory level with the final object, and implied that the save side would automatically follow the read side; there is not enough evidence for either extension.

## Post-review position

The entry point remains `onnx/external_data_helper.py`. That file directly imports `os`, `re`, `sys`, and `uuid`, which makes it suitable for continuing to inspect adjacent code handling external data; the import list itself does not establish a conclusion about directory policy or caller ownership. ONX-212 is retained as a pointer to the field samples and the rule location; the investigation steps on the card are not repeated here.

This round's trial is limited to `_open_external_data_fd`. external_data_helper provides the `_open_external_data_fd` interface, which safely opens external data files within the model directory using file descriptors and rejects symlinks. The discussion of Leaf Link should center on this interface: rather than first committing to have every caller rewrite its path, confirm whether the final open point can preserve and enforce this boundary.

Here, "rejecting symlinks" refers specifically to the final object on this page. If a sample has already passed through Parent Directory Link before reaching that object, don't use this conclusion to count the parent directories as covered as well; troubleshooting could not tell at which layer the rejection occurred.

## What this round tests

The trial compares only two sample classes: an ordinary external data file in the model directory and an external data file whose final object is a symlink. The first is used to verify that consolidating on the interface does not divert normal reads through a bypass; the second is used to verify that the check has not been swallowed by the caller's path preprocessing. The record should include the model directory, the relative location of the external data, the helper interface reached, and the return status. Writing only "A link cannot be read" is not enough to determine whether the issue is at the final object, the parent directory, or the caller's path concatenation.

Leaving the save side out of this round is intentional. Path generation during saving, handling existing files, and the open operation during reading may not share the same boundary. Once the read-side samples are stable, decide whether the save side needs an interface with the same name or only needs to retain the restrictions already in place. Changing both sides together would make it impossible during rollback to tell which side changed ordinary-file behavior.

Nor does this require callers to migrate to a single pattern. The trial first checks whether existing read paths can reach this interface; if a read point does bypass it, record that point and the object it passes in, then discuss whether integration is worthwhile. There is currently no reason to turn a single Leaf Link review into a refactoring plan for all external-data callers.

## Trade-offs

Textual prechecks still have value, especially when a caller wants to provide its own message earlier. But they can only serve as an additional hint; they cannot replace the check at the final open point. The cost of putting the check near the open interface is having to verify that the interface really covers the target read path; the benefit is that the same final object will not be handled differently depending on the caller.

Another option would be to establish a set of path rules covering directories, filenames, and save behavior first, then derive interfaces from those rules. This direction is not adopted. It would bring Parent Directory Link, Regular External File, and the unresolved save-side items into scope together, making the review too broad; these two sample classes also could not determine whether it succeeded.

## Stop conditions

If any one of the following occurs, do not use this proposal to proceed with broader changes:

- An ordinary external data file takes a different read branch because of the final-component check;
- Identifying the final object requires every caller to parse the full path independently first;
- Samples show that the actual issue comes from Parent Directory Link, not from the final path component;
- The interface cannot make clear whether it handles an open operation or a save operation, yet is expected to carry the semantics of both.

Stopping does not mean restoring the old "each caller checks independently" plan. First retain the sample and the branch entered, then move the parent-directory case back to the corresponding page and leave the save side as an unresolved item. If final-component and ordinary-file samples can be distinguished at the same helper interface, only then discuss the form of the error, caller adaptation, and the fixed location for regression samples.

Only three specific questions remain to be confirmed: which existing read paths enter `_open_external_data_fd` directly; what information the upper layer needs to retain on rejection; and whether saving external data encounters the same final object. They do not affect this round's proposal to keep Leaf Link near the open interface, but they will determine whether the trial can move from a local sample to a stable change.

# Parent Directory Link Troubleshooting Tree

The earliest record on this page captured a very narrow case: the model and external data were unchanged, but after the parent directory changed from a regular directory to a link, the status returned by the discovery entry point changed. The value of the old draft is not that it had already explained the cause, but that it required preserving the relative path verbatim. Later, people labeled final-component file links, missing files under regular directories, and Parent Directory Link alike as "link issues," which instead led this record off track.

The starting point is still `onnx/external_data_helper.py`, but do not treat this filename as an explanation of the cause. The old troubleshooting records led here based on issue names and call names; the file shows direct dependencies on `os`, `re`, `sys`, and `uuid`, but that does not establish which branch is responsible for handling paths. Case records should first establish the inputs and statuses, then decide whether to continue tracing the call relationships.

ONX-213 only preserves a limited recheck of this Parent Directory Link: pass the path through the current file discovery entry point, and retain the relative path and the status returned by the tool. The card itself does not interpret the difference as a conclusion about any particular function, so this page does not present it as an implementation defect that has already been located either.

## Separate the Cases First

Here, "Parent Directory Link" means that a directory component before the filename in a relative external data path is a link. For example, a relative path is supplied under the model directory, and an intermediate directory in that path is not a regular directory. This differs from the following two cases:

- The filename itself is a link, while all parent directories are regular directories;
- The path contains no links, but the target file does not exist, permissions are insufficient, or the model directory has changed.

The three cases may produce the same failure status, or they may produce different statuses. Identical statuses do not prove that the same processing path was taken; different statuses cannot be explained away simply by saying "the link was rejected" either. The old draft was overly optimistic on this point: it treated Parent Directory Link as the only variable, but the actual records did not retain enough control inputs.

First copy down these four items, and do not speculate further if any one is missing:

1. The path of the directory containing the model, as observed in the case;
2. The exact relative path supplied to the discovery entry point;
3. Which parent directory in the path is a link, rather than merely writing "contains a link";
4. The status returned by the tool or the original error text.

The exact relative path matters. Collapsing it in advance, converting it to an absolute path, or manually removing `.` and `..` before recording it will erase the differences needed for this check. There is no requirement here to classify every path component as safe or unsafe; the only requirement is to let later readers know what the tool saw.

## Case Branches

```text
Obtain the model directory, relative path, and status
|
+-- Parent directories in the path are not links
|   |
|   +-- The filename is a link
|   |   `-- Go to the Leaf Link record; do not apply this page's conclusions.
|   |
|   `-- No links
|       `-- Check against Regular External File first. If you need to compare with old migration records, see DOC-27.
|
`-- A parent directory in the path is a link
    |
    +-- The exact relative path was not saved
    |   `-- Stop attributing a cause; first add the original path and the tool's return status.
    |
    +-- A regular-directory control exists for the same model and relative path
    |   |
    |   +-- The statuses are the same on both sides
    |   |   `-- Parent Directory Link has not produced a recorded difference, check the target file and model directory.
    |   |
    |   `-- The statuses differ between the two sides
    |       `-- Save both statuses and directory conditions; continue checking the path received by the discovery entry point.
    |
    `-- No regular-directory control
        `-- Only record "status when the parent directory is a link"; do not describe it as a reproduced boundary rule.
```

This tree has more stopping points than the old version. Previously, seeing that the parent directory was a link was enough to continue investigating the link itself; this turned cases without controls into definite conclusions. Now, if the original relative path is missing, or there is no comparable regular-directory condition, the record stops at "what was returned under this condition." It can still be used for later rechecks, but not for a release decision.

## Do Not Reverse the Order

When troubleshooting, first ask where the path was handed to the discovery entry point, and only then ask where it ultimately points in the filesystem. The former is a limited fact this page can retain; without a control from the same case, the latter can easily be replaced by the result of manual resolution. Successfully opening the target file manually does not mean the tool will reach the same location using the same relative path.

Use two lines in the record rather than a single summary sentence:

```text
Relative path supplied: <preserve verbatim>
Tool return status: <preserve verbatim>
```

If a parent directory is a link, add another line identifying the directory component where the link occurs. Do not insert the target's final location back into the first line. This is not about adding more path details, but about avoiding treating "what the input is" and "what the filesystem ultimately resolves it to" as the same object.

When comparing against a regular directory, do not change multiple conditions either. Keep the model directory, relative path, and target file the same; change only the parent directory's directory condition. If the filename, external data contents, or model location is also changed while constructing the control, the result can only be treated as another case and must not overwrite the original record.

The old page included an informal practice: first replace the linked directory with a regular directory, then see whether the problem disappears. This can help obtain a control while on call, but it is not a recovery action, much less an instruction authorizing changes to user directories. A status change after replacement only shows that the tool returns different results under the two directory conditions; an unchanged status after replacement can only rule out an obvious difference in this particular comparison. The old draft described "unchanged" as "unrelated to links"; that judgment is retained here and marked as no longer applicable.

> Deprecated judgment: If a regular directory and Parent Directory Link produce the same status, the path boundary can be considered uninvolved.
>
> Correction: Identical statuses do not show that the two paths underwent the same processing. Without more evidence from the case, only record that the statuses are the same; do not infer that the internal steps are the same.

## What to Check Near the Discovery Entry Point

When the control really does show a status difference, first confirm that the difference occurs at the "current file discovery entry point" layer, rather than appearing only after the model directory has been replaced. This does not require the person investigating the case to read the entire helper; simply compare the relative path supplied at the call site with the original text in the record. If the call site is no longer passing the same string, Parent Directory Link is merely an observable condition and can no longer be treated as the sole variable.

Then ask the following questions in order:

- Does the call site supply a relative path, or a path that has already been converted?
- Is the model directory in the record still the directory from which the model was originally loaded?
- Is the link in a parent directory, or is it actually on the final filename?
- Does the tool status arise during discovery, or only during the later reading stage?

The last item is often the easiest to omit. If all that is known is "cannot open," it is impossible to tell whether the path has already passed through the discovery entry point. Do not describe a general file-read failure as a Parent Directory Link failure just to complete the record; the two must be distinguished using the same set of inputs and statuses.

If the call site is already passing a converted path, this page's investigation stops at the call site. Continuing to speculate about directory handling inside `onnx/external_data_helper.py` adds no new facts at that point. Saving the strings before and after conversion side by side is more useful than adding an explanatory paragraph. If the two are exactly the same, return to the comparison between Parent Directory Link and a regular directory.

## Three Common Wrong Turns

**Treating Leaf Link as Parent Directory Link.** When the filename is a link, all directory components in the path may still be regular directories. The old issue record concerns only the parent-directory condition; attaching results for Leaf Link here would mislead later readers into thinking both entry points had already been checked.

**Rewriting the relative path first.** Some people habitually assemble an absolute path before reproducing the issue to make it easier to inspect the target manually. This action can be included as a note, but it cannot replace the supplied value. The current card requires saving the relative path and the tool's return status precisely because rewriting the path makes it impossible to see the input presented to the discovery entry point.

**Calling a single regular-directory test a fix.** A regular-directory control only helps determine whether the difference changes with the directory condition. It does not establish that links should be accepted, nor does it establish that links should be rejected. The old version's "switch to a regular directory and continue" applied only to the sample temporarily retained at the time and should not be carried over to other models or directory structures.

Of these three, the first remains the most common recording error; the second makes the record lose its value for rechecking; the third misrepresents a control action as operational advice.

## The Minimum Snippet to Retain During a Recheck

When case information is incomplete, leave a short snippet rather than inventing directory details:

```text
Model directory: <value visible in the case>
Relative path: <original text>
Parent Directory Link: <directory component or unconfirmed>
Tool status: <original text>
Regular-directory control: yes / no; if yes, status is <original text>
```

"Unconfirmed" is not a failed record. It means this check cannot yet distinguish Parent Directory Link from other directory conditions. Conversely, if the record contains only a status and no original path text, do not write "Parent Directory Link anomaly" in the title or conclusion either; at most, label it as a path difference pending recheck.

After ONX-213 entered handling, the relative path and status from the current discovery entry point were added back, but no new conclusions were added about Leaf Link, file contents, or model format. This page therefore retains its old, narrow scope: it supports rechecking parent-directory conditions, rather than serving as a handling manual for all external data failures.

## Stopping Conditions That Still Apply

The investigation on this page can end when any one of these conditions is met:

- The current path is confirmed not to contain Parent Directory Link; go to the Regular External File record.
- A final-component file link is confirmed; do not continue applying the parent-directory branch.
- Parent Directory Link is present, but the exact relative path or tool status is missing; complete the record before making a judgment.
- The comparison between a regular directory and Parent Directory Link has been saved, and it is possible to state clearly whether the statuses on the two sides are the same or different; pass the evidence on for a call-site recheck.

Do not append an overall judgment that "links are safe" or "links are unsafe" at the end. The available evidence only supports retaining conditions, inputs, and statuses separately. The path entry point in the old workflow is still useful as a reference, especially when reviewing whether the relative path was rewritten; all other conclusions should be based on new evidence from the call site.

# Compatibility Catalog Consumer FAQ

These three answers were originally left as a quick reference for consumers in the middle of migration. The catalog has its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria; this page has always covered only the public contract around onnx, migration records, and caller compatibility. Not all later cases fit these few answers, but people still come here to find the old entry points.

**Where is the entry point?**

Open `docs/adj-onnx/faq/onnx-compatibility-catalog-three-user-questions.md`. The export marker is `latest-known`. This is treated as the catalog's current revision, so consumers do not need to ask elsewhere for the same content. The body and attachments remain under the compatibility catalog's maintenance.

The entry point name is only used to locate the file; it does not mean that two questions are necessarily about the same issue. When consumers hand a case back, include the specific entry point they opened first; reporting only "compatibility catalog" mixes migration records with caller differences. The catalog's schedule also covers only work within the catalog's scope.

**Do entry points with the same name need to be split?**

The old answer was no. Entries with the same name were to be merged into one current entry point first, with migration notes then added in the same place; recording sources and adopters separately would only create two apparently identical answers. This judgment was also used for questions with similar names but different first visible results.

This approach was retained at the time because consumers mainly needed an entry point they could keep accessing, rather than a table of migration sources. If two pieces of material appeared under the same name, they were still to be written in the same place first; this page did not go into who adopted it first or who maintained it. A matching name alone was treated as sufficient grounds for merging.

**What should be submitted first for similar symptoms?**

Provide the specific entry point, the time of occurrence, and a minimal sample that distinguishes the two cases. Keep the original input, the revision used, and the first visible result together. If there is only a screenshot without this information, the case can be kept on file temporarily, but it should not be used to judge long-term compatibility implications.

Preserve the first result as the caller actually saw it; do not replace it with cleaned-up migration notes first. Publicly visible differences and access scope are not the same thing; the former helps determine which entry point a question belongs under, while the latter only says who could view the material left at the time. Combining these two kinds of records will lead later owners to mistakenly think a compatibility relationship has already been confirmed.

**Can the material be mixed together?**

Record publicly visible results, access scope, and follow-up handling separately. Cleaned-up records must not overwrite the original input; migration notes must not replace the differences the caller first saw. There is no conclusion yet on whether another independent source exists.

**Who handles it next?**

The person on duty first determines whether the issue is still within the compatibility catalog's scope. A temporary owner handles only actions that are due and does not write up long-term implications on someone else's behalf; when the issue crosses into a shared interface, hand only the reproduction entry point to the relevant maintainer. A minimal sample is enough for the handoff; do not forward the full migration background. For unresolved cases, see DOC-31.

# Compatibility Directory Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

This tree preserves what was then the current entry-point state. If you encounter "onnx-compatibility-catalog is stuck," first record where it stopped, the first failing sample, and the environment differences at the time; don't refresh the page or rerun the entire path first. The old records include one case where retrying too soon meant the initial rejection point wasn't captured, leaving only guesses afterward about whether the entry point or the directory contents were at fault.

First check whether the entry point can still return the first result.

- The entry point itself doesn't exist, or access is denied before entering the directory: don't classify this as onnx-compatibility-catalog. Keep the original entry-point location and rejection point, hand it off to whoever maintains permissions for that entry point, and stop here.
- You can enter the directory, but no further result is produced at a particular object: continue checking the local records. Here, "no further result" refers only to a reproducible stopping point, not version-conversion conclusions filled in from memory.

Look for `parser` starting from `docs/adj-onnx/runbooks/onnx-compatibility-catalog-blocked-escalation-contacts.md`. This is the starting point of the old tree: if the path can't be found, don't continue by substituting a similarly named directory, and don't treat the old link as proof that the parser has run. Also record the location of the page you actually opened, then return to the permissions branch.

After finding `parser`, first check whether `quoted identifier` has appeared.

- It has: don't clear the state, and don't replace the identifier with a plain name and retry. Keep the original spelling and continue checking for `data propagation` farther along.
- It hasn't: this old procedure does not allow you to skip past the parser and conclude that the compatibility directory contents no longer work. Stop at the input or page location before the parser; if that location is permission-restricted, route it to the permissions maintainers.

If `data propagation` hasn't appeared, stop here. The old records treat this branch as a signal that the directory side needs more evidence, not as a failure that can be handed straight to version conversion. Bring only the first failing sample, the environment differences, and the layer where it stopped to the directory maintainers; if you don't have these, collect a sample first, and don't broaden the investigation.

If `data propagation` has appeared, the old procedure uses "version conversion" as the next handoff destination. This was the handoff practice at the time, not confirmation that the conversion layer was the cause. When handing off, state that it has already gone through the parser, give the status of `quoted identifier`, and say where propagation appeared; if the directory maintainers need new evidence, this tree does not make further inferences on their behalf.

Don't combine an access denial and a directory stall in the same report. Send the former to the entry-point permissions maintainers and the latter to the onnx-compatibility-catalog maintainers; if neither side can confirm, retain the first failing sample and exit. Don't substitute repeated access attempts for an assessment.

The recovery actions have not been tried in a shared environment. The parts of the old records that list "version conversion" as the final destination are still kept for navigation. If the entry point changes later, the new path should be recorded separately, without overwriting this old tree.
