# Documentation Site Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When the documentation site got stuck, the earliest records only asked "can the current entry point be opened". Later, when taking over the old records, it became clear that this wording conflated the entry point, `workflow-scripts-documentation-portal`, page content, release notes, and the account environment. The old two-way split is retained below so that whoever takes over can see why issues used to be sent to the wrong place; it is not a description of the documentation site's current state.

The earliest approach was: if the documentation site was visible at the entry point, keep clicking; if a retry turned green, end that troubleshooting session. This action did not preserve the page from the first failure, nor did it establish which part of the flow the user had originally gone through. `C++ extension`, `Python binding`, and `FunctionProto` in the old entry-point file were once treated as signposts for further troubleshooting, but there was no material showing that they belonged to the same blocking point. These terms can now only be retained with the original records, and cannot route a branch to a particular owner on their own.

When taking over, first record four things directly observable in the current situation: what the current entry point displays, whether `workflow-scripts-documentation-portal` has been reached, whether page content appears before or after the release notes, and which environment the account is in. The documentation site may contain docs, guide, and release notes at the same time; one object displaying correctly does not prove that another object is working correctly. A page opening later also cannot erase the first point where the user could not continue.

```text
The user says "the documentation site is stuck"
│
├─ The current entry point does not display the documentation site
│  │
│  ├─ The entry-point display differs from the existing records
│  │  └─ Record the display location and current revision; stop on the entry-point side
│  │
│  └─ There is only a statement of "cannot see it", with no page record
│     └─ Do not send the issue to portal or guess about permissions
│
├─ Reached workflow-scripts-documentation-portal
│  │
│  ├─ Page content is missing, or does not match the release notes
│  │  ├─ The first difference can be identified
│  │  │  └─ Keep it on the documentation-site maintenance side, retaining docs, guide, and release notes
│  │  └─ The only description is "it looks wrong"
│  │     └─ First add the specific location on the page; the tree stops here
│  │
│  ├─ The content is visible, but the user cannot continue
│  │  ├─ The account, environment, and stopping point are all available
│  │  │  ├─ The account has no permissions in this environment
│  │  │  │  └─ Hand off to the permissions owner, retaining the initial symptom on the documentation-site side
│  │  │  └─ There is no record of a permissions anomaly
│  │  │     └─ Do not describe it as a permissions issue, return to the page-content branch
│  │  └─ Account or environment information is missing
│  │     └─ Stop here, waiting for the original records
│  │
│  └─ The page and subsequent actions are all complete
│     └─ Exit this investigation; retain the earlier failed page and environment
│
└─ It is unclear whether portal was entered
   └─ Record only the current entry point until the first stopping point can be identified
```

The statement "the entry point can be opened" in the old records is no longer used to judge whether the documentation site is working correctly. The entry point only shows that the user saw the entry-point layer; it does not show that the pages in portal, the release notes, or the account permissions are already usable. Conversely, the issue cannot be attributed to the documentation site when there is no entry-point record either. If there is no page record on the entry-point side, the tree stops on the entry-point side, without writing up the later page branches as events that have already happened.

After entering portal, first separate page content from release notes. Missing page content does not mean that old release notes are still present; outdated release notes do not mean that the user actually stopped at the release notes. docs, guide, and release notes may come from different times. Whoever takes over only needs to identify which object the user stopped at, and the first difference between that location and the content at hand. When no first difference has been identified, do not infer which content the user read from directory names.

If the current page has reached portal but the old release notes are still there, first preserve the two locations side by side. The old content itself is a documentation-site maintenance issue and must not be overwritten just to make the page look consistent. The documentation site has its own maintenance arrangements, and handling outdated content does not automatically resolve the stoppage on the entry-point side; only treat it as a page branch in this tree after confirming that the user stopped next to those old notes.

ONXD-007 document a narrow condition: when only the adjacent workflow-scripts-documentation-portal is replaced, the current entry point and current revision are still read from the same entry point. This can answer the narrow question "the adjacent object changed, did the entry point change along with it". It does not prove that a single adjacent replacement affects all users, nor does it prove that this blockage was caused by an entry-point switch. If a difference in an adjacent object happens to appear in the current situation, first save that difference, then compare it side by side with the first page stoppage; without the original page location, the tree does not extend further.

This also changes the old comparison method. In the past, some people would go back and rerun the entry point when they saw an adjacent object change, treating the green rerun result as meaning that the entry point was not involved. Now, the rerun result is recorded only as a later page state. It can be placed alongside the original failure, but cannot overwrite it; if the entry-point display was not retained before the rerun, the rerun result cannot reconstruct whether the user actually entered portal at that time either.

The execution records for ONXD-008 already have samples attached, but there is still a gap in the intervening troubleshooting history. The reason later recorded for the blockage was that the account supplied by the caller had no permissions in this environment. This result shows that permissions can be a branch, not that every case of "content is visible but the user cannot continue" is a permissions issue. Only when the account, environment, and point where the user cannot continue all match should the page evidence be handed off to the permissions owner; if any one is missing, retain it as a page branch that has not yet been classified.

When the account is not in the expected environment, there is no need to rewrite the documentation-site content first. First retain the page location and the environment the account is in, then confirm whether that account actually reached portal. If the account did not reach portal, the permissions branch has no starting point; if it did reach portal and a first difference exists in the page content itself, the content branch must not be skipped just because a permissions issue also exists. The two issues can be recorded side by side, but cannot substitute for each other.

The review requirements on the same card once listed a maintenance entry point, an exit action, and a rollback action. In this tree, maintenance entry point means that the old documentation-site path can still be found; exit action means explicitly stating whether troubleshooting stopped at the entry point, a page difference, or the account environment; rollback action appears only when changes need to be reverted on the documentation-site side. The records have not filled in the intervening gap, so the review cannot be written up as a confirmed account of the root cause.

The old tree's "exit if the user can continue" is still retained, but it was often interpreted as permission to clear away failure evidence. Here, exiting only means that this path will not be extended further. The entry-point display, page location, account environment, and content differences from the first failure should still be retained; another run turning green can only serve as a new observation. It cannot turn a branch that originally lacked evidence into a confirmed cause.

Issues with the documentation site's own resources, permissions, or index can continue to be handled within the project. When entry-point conventions outside the documentation site need to change, this page stops where new evidence is required, rather than deciding the destination for adjacent projects. This stopping point is especially applicable to descriptions such as "it can already be opened, but the user cannot continue": first confirm whether the stopping point is the page, the release notes, or the account environment, then discuss whether a handoff is needed.

When taking over, still start from `docs/adj-workflow-scripts/runbooks/workflow-scripts-documentation-portal-blocked-escalation-contacts.md`. This path is the entry point for the old records of workflow scripts · Documentation Portal, and that project maintains the body and attachments. For general questions about usage entry points, refer to DOC-42; when the situation includes "already opened but cannot continue", inconsistent release notes, or an account-environment blockage, retain the first stopping point recorded on this page. Do not retroactively write up the outcome after handoff as a cause that was already known at the time.

# Troubleshooting Quality Signal Dashboard failures

Applies to a third-party-quality-signal run that has already failed. Preserve the run state first, then confirm where it stopped when it failed; don't set up another run just to get a complete set of results.

## Inspect the failed run

Open the corresponding record from `docs/adj-third-party/runbooks/third-party-quality-signal-board-failed-run-on-call-page.md` and find "Version conversion" on the page. First copy the original command text already shown there, the timestamp, and the current revision; don't fill in missing parameters from memory. If there's another generation record, first compare the commands and timestamps side by side, and note only the earliest point where they diverge.

If the run has already gone through `opset`, do not clean the working directory, overwrite the original output, or append anything from a retry to the original log. `opset` is only a reference point; it doesn't establish that version conversion has completed or that the cause of the failure has been determined.

## First stopping point

Check whether `TensorProto` appears around version conversion.

- Not present: stop here. Save the last log segment you saw and the exit code, and record "No TensorProto seen before version conversion." Do not continue investigating GraphProto, external data, or symbolic links.
- Present: preserve the context in which it appears, then look only at the first failure output immediately after it. Later repeated errors do not count as the first location of this failure.
- The command parameters on the page don't match the run state: leave the original record unchanged; put the newly supplied parameters and their results on a separate line so they don't look like part of the original run.

If the earliest divergence is between two generation records, first state clearly which one changed first, then stop trying to attribute a cause. Without an established order, neither difference can be treated as the cause of the failure.

## What to save after stopping

Before handing back the current revision, save the exit code, the Quality Signal Dashboard name, and the final log segment. If only truncated output remains in the log, preserve it as is; do not replace it with a summary. Put the following in the same handoff record:

- The page entry point for this run;
- Whether the original command is complete and, if not, which parameters are missing;
- Whether the first confirmable point is the absence of `opset` or `TensorProto`, or the first failure after that;
- The saved exit code and final log segment;
- Whether the environment has been handed back.

Recovery actions have not yet been tried in the shared environment. After reaching the stopping points above, do not attempt recovery by cleaning up, rerunning, or replacing the output; retain the original entry point and records of the failure state in the handoff, and let the person who maintains that entry point decide whether to start a separate run.

# IR-18 Freeze Window FAQ

The freeze-window questions for IR-18 never went away; the old answers just lumped them together as "the entry point passed." A later review separated the samples, candidate paths, and working tree. This page still retains the old guidance because people may use it to decide whether the window can be closed out. The claim that "once it's green, we can close" can no longer be used as written.

## What does the schema-export entry point tell us?

An existing successful sample passing through the schema-export entry point only shows that this sample did not fail on this export path. It is not an overall assessment of the candidate path, nor does it cover adjacent rejection samples. The entry-point result can be retained, but it does not expand the scope of the finding.

The old record said, "Once the entry point is green, we can close out." That was a shortcut answer recorded when the rejection samples had not been reviewed alongside it, and it was later overturned. Writing a successful result directly as a compatibility conclusion treats untested combinations as acceptable by default. That should not be recorded during the freeze window.

Adjacent rejection samples are not just another way to confirm the successful sample. They answer whether the boundary still rejects those cases. Success and rejection results must be reviewed together; the former cannot replace the latter. If either has not been run, the record must remain unresolved, with no speculative conclusion added.

## Who withdraws the candidate path?

Withdrawing a candidate path is not a side effect of checking the entry point. When a candidate is proposed, the withdrawal action and the person responsible for carrying it out should both be recorded. Without those two items, even an entry-point maintainer who has seen the export result may not know where the candidate was proposed or who should remove it from the scope of this closeout.

The old answer assigned this to the entry-point maintainer by default because they were the first to see the entry-point status. That seemed convenient in the rush to freeze, but it left a gap: the candidate path might have come from elsewhere, while the entry-point maintainer only had the successful sample. That default assignment no longer applies and cannot be used to fill a responsibility gap.

Withdrawal here means removing the candidate path from the scope of this closeout, not deleting an existing successful sample. A cleaned-up working tree only shows that local changes have been cleared. It does not prove that the withdrawal action has been documented, much less replace confirmation from the person carrying it out.

## Under what conditions can we close?

Before closing, check the successful sample, adjacent rejection samples, and cleaned-up working tree together. If any of the three is missing, the combination remains marked as unresolved, not compatible by default. This sequence explains why looking only at the schema-export entry point is not enough to answer the closure question: the entry-point result covers only one sample, and the working tree reflects only local changes.

Questions about the filesystem fixture can be logged, but there is no result here. The existing samples did not exercise it; that does not mean this boundary has passed, nor should it be turned into a freeze blocker. The build queue's single-variable rerun is recorded in DOC-50. That note only retains the queue rerun and does not replace this page's assessment of samples, withdrawal, and closure conditions.

# Cross-Group On-Call Handoff Decision Record

The initial record left behind only an easily misread conclusion: keep the entry point for now and keep moving the window forward. Only when this sentence was broken down again during review did we realize that the disagreement was not about "whether to add compatibility," but about what could serve as a stable point of comparison during the handoff. If the current entry point, window scope, and implementation combination all change at once, on-call staff have no way to explain which layer caused a difference observed by the caller.

This time, we decided to retain the current update-plan entry point while advancing the compatibility window as a separate effort. Retaining it leaves a position that can be reverted to during the handoff; it does not announce that the old entry point remains the long-term default path, nor does it mean that it already covers all legacy models. The window can continue to be adjusted within the scope supported by available evidence, while whether to withdraw the entry point will be revisited only after it no longer serves to explain differences.

## Options Considered at the Time

The first option was to retain the entry point and tighten the window separately. This minimized changes to the entry point, so callers still had a path back to the original determination; the window would then be adjusted incrementally according to the boundaries already observed. The cost was that both the old entry point and the new window would exist during the handoff, so the record could not simply say "switched." On-call staff would first need to determine where the caller actually went, and then assess whether the window's result applied to that call.

The second option was to replace the entry point and the window together. Supporters of this option believed that a single switch would be easier to explain externally and would reduce the amount of legacy-path maintenance. However, it tied together two different concerns: the window is responsible for the compatibility scope, while the entry point is responsible for the handoff destination. If either result failed, the rollback would take the other back with it, making it difficult later to reconstruct from a single failure whether the impact was in the schema, text, or file boundary.

Another view was to leave everything unchanged temporarily and adjust only after the behavior of all legacy models had been confirmed. This view did not become the decision. It would indeed reduce switching activity, but it would also freeze the scope for which rerun evidence already existed. The meeting retained a narrower approach: scopes with evidence enter review, while legacy-model behavior without evidence continues to be recorded separately as unknown.

## What to Check First During the Handoff

First look at the three surfaces observable by the caller, rather than starting at the implementation layers and deciding that "it should be fine." The schema is the first comparison point; if the text representation changes, that must also be recorded separately; and the file boundary cannot be compressed into the statement "the file can be read." These three surfaces do not represent the same conclusion. The fact that a model can be read only shows that the entry point completed the read this time; it does not also prove that the text output and file boundary match the window's expectations.

When the implementation requires combining the Python and C++ layers, a pass in only one layer cannot serve as the handoff conclusion. The Python-side result can help locate what the caller actually saw, and the C++-side result can show whether the other part of the combination holds, but differences may still remain between them. The handoff record must place each difference back on the corresponding schema, text, or file observation surface; when there is insufficient evidence, it must not be rewritten as meaning that the window already covers it.

This sequence is intended to resolve on-site judgment, not to add a new process for every caller. First fix the visible boundaries, then discuss how the implementation is combined, and only afterward discuss whether the old entry point can be withdrawn. If the entry point is withdrawn first and the window is checked later, there will be no old position to return to when a failure occurs; if the entry point is merely retained without advancing the window, existing evidence will not become a new compatibility determination.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Retain update-plan old entry point] --> B[Fix the schema, text, and file boundaries]
    B --> C[Review the Python and C++ combination]
    C --> D{Is there rerun evidence for the legacy-model behavior}
    D -->|Yes| E[Proceed with window adjustment]
    D -->|No| F[Retain the unknowns and original samples]
    E --> G[Discuss withdrawing the old entry point afterward]
    F --> G
```

The convergence in the diagram does not mean automatic withdrawal. It means that the window and the unknown items have each been reviewed separately, making it possible to revisit the status of the entry point. While the old entry point exists, it cannot be treated as proof of the new window; likewise, a change to the window cannot support the inference that the old entry point is no longer useful.

## The Boundary Actually Approved This Time

What was approved was the limited scope supported by the available evidence. The record must describe the schema, text, and file boundaries observed by the caller and be traceable to the corresponding version, environment, and CI job. The version is required because the same model can exhibit different behavior in different conversion states; the environment is required because a local result does not automatically represent the handoff environment; and the CI job is required because without an execution location, there is no way to know whether the failure node belongs to this window.

Screenshots and old links can help locate an entry point that was used in the past, but they cannot independently serve as evidence that the window covers it. During review, an old link was initially understood to mean "this path has already been validated," but we later found that it only proved that the entry point had been used; it did not show that the schema, text, and file boundaries within the same window had all been checked. This assessment remains in the historical material, while the conclusion has been changed to: usage records for the old entry point and confirmation records for the compatibility scope must be considered separately.

Therefore, work continues within the scope covered by existing evidence, rather than stopping everything because of unconfirmed behavior in legacy models. Conversely, a legacy model cannot be automatically classified as compatible merely because it falls within a similar window. Behavior without rerun evidence retains its original sample and clues for re-execution; a currently confirmed set of results cannot vouch for similar but unchecked models. Handoff personnel need to understand the difference between these two types of records; otherwise, when the next difference appears, they can only guess again whether it is a known change or an old unknown item.

The coordinator is responsible for keeping the entry-point status, window changes, and withdrawal discussion on the same handoff path, but does not confirm specific results on behalf of every caller. If a difference appears only on the Python side, it cannot be written directly as meaning that the C++ combination has passed; if the C++ side has a partial pass, that cannot complete confirmation of the text and file boundaries. The coordinator's responsibility is to preserve these branches and allow the corresponding evidence to continue returning to its own version, environment, and CI job.

## Why the Old Entry Point Is Not Being Withdrawn Yet

Directly removing update-plan creates two problems. First, while the window is still being adjusted, a new difference observed by the caller would cause thecurrentsite to lose both the old entry point and the comparison position at the same time; second, withdrawing the entry point could be mistaken for completion of the window, even though unconfirmed legacy models still exist. Retaining the old entry point keeps recovery actions separate from diagnostic actions and at least prevents a single withdrawal from deleting the original reference point as well.

However, retaining it also has clear limits. It must not be presented as part of the new window, treated as a long-term route for all callers, or used as a reason to skip checks of the schema, text, and file boundaries. If someone still handles an issue through the old entry point during the handoff, that fact must be recorded; it shows that the entry point still has practical value, not that the window's scope has automatically expanded.

The withdrawal discussion must consider several things together: the approved scope has a corresponding version, environment, and CI job; changes to the schema, text, and file boundaries can be explained separately; the Python and C++ combination no longer needs to rely on the old entry point for diagnosis; and legacy models that have not been rerun remain recorded as unknown rather than being silently folded into the window. These are not a new release commitment, but the basis for determining whether the old entry point is still carrying handoff responsibilities. If evidence is missing for any one of them, withdrawal will turn an unknown into an indistinguishable failure.

## Statements That Were Not Adopted

"Switch everything first, then see where it fails" was not adopted. It treats failure as the first record of the boundary, so the result seen by the caller would mix entry-point changes with window changes. When a problem occurred, we could only guess at the previous state again and could not determine whether the schema had changed, the text output had changed, or the file boundary had been handled differently.

"Wait until all legacy models have been confirmed before changing anything" was also not adopted. This statement puts unknown and known items on the same waiting track, meaning that the scope covered by existing evidence has no opportunity to be tightened further. The decision is not to require legacy models to produce a unified answer immediately, but to retain the unknowns and allow confirmed subsets to continue into window review.

"Only looking at the Python side is enough" and "looking only at the C++ side is more reliable" were both rejected. The former misses cross-layer combinations, while the latter postpones examination of the text and file boundaries actually seen by the caller until there is no reference point. Both layers must participate in the assessment, but a partial success in one layer must not be written as meaning that the other layer is complete.

## The Handoff Record's Point of Record

For each new observation, first state which surface it changed: the schema, the text, or the file boundary; then state whether it affects the window; and only afterward state whether the old entry point still needs to be retained. This prevents a local difference from being amplified into "the compatibility work is complete" or "the entire window has failed." If the evidence lacks a version, environment, or CI job, record it only as a clue requiring verification and do not expand the approved scope.

The review also retained a practical trade-off: the record should put caller impact first and implementation combinations second; this lets handoff personnel see the external boundaries that must be protected before tracing the reasons for the Python and C++ combination. Convenience at the implementation layer cannot replace the result observed by the caller, and the convenience of the old entry point cannot replace the window boundary.

DOC-52 later took over the handoff details of the switching process. This record preserves the options compared during the handoff, the reasons for retaining the old entry point, and the judgments that must continue to be kept separate. The window can continue to change, and unknowns can also be reduced one by one; until these two matters can be independently reviewed, withdrawing the entry point cannot be written as a synonym for completing the window.

# IR-18 Freeze Window Switching Notes

The handoff artifacts for the freeze window have not changed: they are still the current sample, version, and owner. The review changed the order of assessment. The initial draft started with "find a consumer that can roll back on its own." That trial run is still included, but it cannot replace an inventory of known write-parse consumers and their old entry points. A successful run through the candidate path only shows that this one consumer completed a round trip with the existing handoff artifacts. It does not show that the other calls have migrated.

The window does not require all consumers to leave the old entry points at the same time. First list the write-parse consumers that can currently be confirmed, with the old entry point each depends on written right next to it. "Known" here only means the calling surface already counted by the person handing off; it does not mean there are no consumers outside the list. When someone reports an additional consumer, add it to the list first. Even if it is not taking part in this round's trial run, it must not disappear from the record just because it is not being handled yet.

Maintain the list by handoff subject, not by candidate path. Each row should show at least the following:

|Consumer|Current sample|Version|Old entry point|Owner|Rollback action|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|Known consumer|Sample included in this handoff|Version currently in use|Entry point still in use|Person who will continue filling in the record|Action to return to that entry point|

This table is not meant to write a complete migration guide on the consumer's behalf. It brings together the subjects that can be checked in this round: the sample and version identify the subject of the trial run, the old entry point identifies where recovery must return, and the owner identifies who will keep the record updated when a new consumer or a mismatch appears. If any cell is empty, leave that gap visible; do not fill it with information from an adjacent consumer.

The candidate consumer must still be a consumer that can roll back on its own. It first checks whether the sample and version it received are the current ones in the list, then confirms that ownership has remained continuous through the handoff. An old sample cannot stand in for the current sample. Waiting until after the switch to find someone who can restore the old entry point does not count as a completed handoff either. Write down the rollback action before switching, and make sure it can return this consumer to its originally recorded old entry point.

```text
Before switching
Known consumer ──> Old entry point
       │
       └── Current sample / Version / Owner

After the candidate switch
Candidate consumer ──> Candidate path
       │
       └── Roll back independently ──> Original old entry point
```

The two paths in the diagram only describe the handoff sequence within the window. They do not indicate that the old entry point has been decommissioned. Once the candidate consumer reaches the candidate path, check two distinct things: first, whether the current sample and version still match the list; second, whether the documented rollback action actually points to the original old entry point. A mismatch in the first means the subject of this trial run is no longer clear. If the second is missing, the candidate path cannot be used as a basis for switching, even if it is temporarily usable.

Rollback does not need to wait for a larger failure. If any one of the sample, version, or owner does not match, the candidate consumer returns to the old entry point first, then records the mismatch in the corresponding row. Do not clear the owner column after restoring the old entry point. The contacts from before and after the switch remain leads for follow-up questions when filling out the calling surface. If the old entry point is maintained elsewhere, this page retains only the entry point and the current contact; it does not write unreviewed conclusions on the other party's behalf.

This review also tightened how handoff records are written. A record can state who is doing the trial run, what current sample they brought, which version it corresponds to, and where they return on rollback. Judgments that have not been reviewed must not be written as conclusions for the window. The page can leave items unconfirmed for a time, especially when a newly reported consumer does not yet have an old entry point recorded. Filling the list with guesses would make it impossible for the next trial run to distinguish between validating the candidate path and endorsing an unconfirmed old path.

The two gaps are handled differently. When a known consumer has no old entry point recorded, add the entry point first and do not classify that row as a completed switch yet. When a candidate consumer has a sample, version, and owner but no rollback action it can execute on its own, stop before switching and retain the old entry point. The first gap affects the inventory of the calling surface; the second affects the candidate trial run. Neither can be covered by saying "the candidate path works."

The search for the build queue maintenance entry point is recorded separately in DOC-53. That record can help locate the entry point for later maintenance, but it does not automatically fill out the consumer list here. Even if the maintenance entry point is found, checks must still be made against the old entry point and rollback action on this page. The location of an entry point and whether a particular consumer has completed a round-trip switch are two different things.

Proceed with this round's handoff in the following order:

1. Update the known write-parse consumers and record the old entry points each still uses.
2. Add newly reported consumers to the list first. If their old entry points have not yet been identified, do not let them into the candidate trial run's completion record.
3. Check the current sample, version, and owner for the candidate consumer, confirming that these handoff artifacts refer to the same trial-run subject.
4. Before switching, write down a rollback action that this consumer can execute on its own and that returns it to its original old entry point.
5. Have the candidate consumer take the candidate path. If the sample, version, or owner does not match, restore the old entry point first, then fill the gaps in the list.
6. Retain newly added consumers and unconfirmed items. Do not mark the window complete prematurely just because one consumer has completed the trial run.

Whether the window remains marked as migration in progress depends only on two actual gaps: known consumers have not all been counted, or the candidate consumer has no rollback action. If either gap remains, retain the old entry point, and have the owners in the list continue maintaining the handoff.
